notes.title: Clock arithmetic: the mod operator
notes.body:
a mod n is the remainder when a is divided by n. 17 mod 5 = 2. Clocks are mod 12: 10 + 5 = 3 (o'clock) because 15 mod 12 = 3. The key property: you can reduce mod n at ANY point in a computation - (a+b) mod n = ((a mod n)+(b mod n)) mod n, and the same for multiplication. This is what lets cryptography work with 2048-bit numbers: reduce early, reduce often.

Worked example (with solution):
Compute (47 x 53) mod 7 without a calculator doing 47x53.
47 mod 7 = 5 (42 is divisible by 7). 53 mod 7 = 4 (49 divisible). (5 x 4) mod 7 = 20 mod 7 = 6. Answer: 6.
Verify: 47x53 = 2491; 2491 / 7 = 355.857...; 355x7 = 2485; 2491-2485 = 6. Correct.

Negative mods: -3 mod 7 = 4 (add 7 until positive). In PowerShell, -3 % 7 gives -3 (truncated), so crypto code normalizes: (($x % $n) + $n) % $n.

notes.title: Diffie-Hellman with pocket numbers
notes.body:
Two strangers agree on public prime p and base g, each picks a secret, and they derive a SHARED secret over a public channel. The magic: (g^a)^b mod p = (g^b)^a mod p = g^(ab) mod p. An eavesdropper sees g, p, and the public values but cannot feasibly recover a or b (the discrete logarithm problem).

Worked example (with solution):
Public: p = 23, g = 5. Alice secret a = 6, Bob secret b = 15.
Alice public: 5^6 mod 23. 5^2=25->2; 5^4 = 2^2=4; 5^6 = 5^4 x 5^2 = 4x2 = 8 mod 23. Alice sends 8.
Bob public: 5^15 mod 23. 5^8 = 4^2 = 16; 5^15 = 5^8 x 5^4 x 5^2 x 5^1 = 16x4x2x5 = 640 mod 23. 23x27=621; 640-621=19. Bob sends 19.
Shared: Alice computes 19^6 mod 23; Bob computes 8^15 mod 23. Both equal 5^(6x15) mod 23 = 5^90 mod 23.
Compute 5^90 mod 23: order of 5 mod 23 divides 22; 5^11 mod 23? 5^2=2,5^4=4,5^8=16, 5^11=5^8*5^2*5=16*2*5=160 mod 23 = 160-138=22 = -1. So 5^22 = 1, 5^90 = 5^(88+2) = 1 x 25 mod 23 = 2.
Shared secret = 2. Verify Alice: 19^6 mod 23: 19 = -4; (-4)^2=16; (-4)^4=16^2=256 mod 23 = 256-253=3; (-4)^6 = 3x16=48 mod 23 = 2. Correct - both sides get 2 without ever sending it.

notes.title: Toy RSA: encryption you can check by hand
notes.body:
RSA: pick primes p, q; n = p*q; choose e coprime to (p-1)(q-1); find d with e*d mod (p-1)(q-1) = 1. Public key (e, n) encrypts: c = m^e mod n. Private key d decrypts: m = c^d mod n. Security rests on factoring n being hard when n is huge; with toy primes you can watch every step.

Worked example (with solution):
 p = 3, q = 11 -> n = 33, phi = (3-1)(11-1) = 20. Choose e = 3 (coprime to 20). Find d: 3d mod 20 = 1 -> d = 7 (21 mod 20 = 1).
Encrypt m = 5: c = 5^3 mod 33 = 125 mod 33. 33x3=99; 125-99=26. c = 26.
Decrypt: m = 26^7 mod 33. 26 = -7. (-7)^2=49 mod 33=16. (-7)^4 = 16^2=256 mod 33: 33x7=231, 256-231=25. (-7)^7 = (-7)^4 x (-7)^2 x (-7) = 25x16x(-7) mod 33. 25x16=400 mod 33: 33x12=396, remainder 4. 4x(-7) = -28 mod 33 = 5. m = 5. Round trip verified.

Real RSA uses 2048-bit n; the math is identical, only the numbers are astronomical. Password hashing (bcrypt/Argon2) and TLS key exchange both live on modular arithmetic.

notes.title: Sets, Venn diagrams, and the five operations
notes.body:
A set is a collection of distinct things. A = {users in Finance}, B = {laptop owners}. Union A u B: in either. Intersection A n B: in both. Difference A - B: in A but not B. Complement A': everything not in A. Subset A c B: every member of A is in B.

Venn diagrams make these visual: two overlapping circles; the lens is the intersection, the crescent is the difference. Inclusion-exclusion counts the union without double-counting: |A u B| = |A| + |B| - |A n B|.

Worked example (with solution):
200 users: 120 in Finance (F), 90 own laptops (L), 60 are in both.
Only Finance (F - L) = 120 - 60 = 60. Only laptops (L - F) = 90 - 60 = 30. Both = 60. Neither = 200 - (60+30+60) = 50.
Check via inclusion-exclusion: |F u L| = 120 + 90 - 60 = 150; neither = 200 - 150 = 50. Consistent.

notes.title: AD groups are sets (nesting is subset)
notes.body:
An AD security group IS a set of principals. Nesting group G2 inside G1 makes G2 a subset of G1's effective membership: every member of G2 is effectively in G1. Token bloat, the classic AD headache, is inclusion-exclusion failing you: a user's token lists every group in their transitive closure, and deeply nested groups multiply SIDs.

Circular nesting (A in B, B in A) is legal in AD and means A and B have identical effective membership - the sets are equal. AGDLP (Accounts -> Global -> Domain Local -> Permissions) is a set pipeline: each stage is a subset relationship that keeps the permission sets manageable.

Worked example (with solution):
G_Helpdesk has 8 direct users. G_Support contains G_Helpdesk plus 4 direct users. G_Admins contains G_Support plus 2 direct users.
Effective members: |G_Helpdesk| = 8. |G_Support| = 8 + 4 = 12 (subsets don't double count). |G_Admins| = 12 + 2 = 14.
If you grant 'log on as batch' to G_Admins, the affected set is exactly those 14 - audit by expanding the transitive closure, never by eyeballing direct members.

notes.title: GPO scope as set operations
notes.body:
A GPO applies to: (objects under linked OUs/Site/Domain) INTERSECT (security filtering: Authenticated Users or listed groups with Apply permission) INTERSECT (WMI filter true) MINUS (deny Apply permission) MINUS (Block Inheritance, unless Enforced). That single sentence predicts every 'why didn't my policy apply' ticket.

Deny beats allow in security filtering: the effective set is (Allow set) - (Deny set). An 'exception group' pattern is literally set difference: policy applies to All_Laptops minus Kiosk_Devices.

Worked example (with solution):
GPO linked to OU=Sales (300 computer objects). Security filtering: GG_Sales_Laptops (180 members, all in OU=Sales). WMI filter: SELECT * FROM Win32_OperatingSystem WHERE Version LIKE '10.%' (matches 150 of the 180). Deny group: GG_NoPolicy (10 members, all in the 150).
Applied set = 300 n 180 n 150 - 10 = 150 - 10 = 140 computers.
If the helpdesk asks 'why didn't it hit PC-77', check each set in order: in OU? in GG_Sales_Laptops? OS match? in deny group? The first 'no' is the answer - set logic turns guessing into a checklist.

notes.title: Common mistakes: Set Theory: AD Groups & GPO Logic
notes.body:
**The mistakes that create repeat tickets — and the discipline that prevents them.**

- **Skipping the physical layer.** Half of 'network issues' and 'dead machines' are power, cabling, or seating. Check the boring causes first, in order, every time.
- **Changing three things at once.** Shotgun troubleshooting means you never learn what actually fixed it — and the problem comes back. One change, one test.
- **No baseline documentation.** If you don't know what 'normal' looks like for this system, you can't recognize abnormal. Document baselines when things work.
- **Permissions by guesswork.** Granting admin rights to 'make it work' creates tomorrow's breach. Diagnose the actual permission required and grant exactly that.
- **Closing the ticket without verifying.** The fix that wasn't tested is a reopen waiting to happen. Reproduce the original symptom and confirm it's gone.

notes.body:

notes.title: Availability: the one formula
notes.body:
Availability A = MTBF / (MTBF + MTTR). MTBF (mean time between failures) measures reliability; MTTR (mean time to repair) measures recoverability. A system that fails yearly but recovers in an hour: A = 8760 / 8761 = 99.9886%. A system that fails monthly but recovers in 5 minutes: A = 730 / 730.083 = 99.9886%. Same nines, totally different operational feel - the second one pages you 12x more often.

Unavailability U = 1 - A. Downtime per year = U x 8760 hours. Memorize the nines: 99% = 3.65 days/yr (87.6h); 99.9% = 8.76h/yr (43.8 min/month); 99.95% = 4.38h/yr (21.9 min/month); 99.99% = 52.6 min/yr (4.38 min/month); 99.999% = 5.26 min/yr.

Worked example (with solution):
A file server has MTBF = 2000 hours, MTTR = 4 hours. Availability?
A = 2000 / 2004 = 0.998004 = 99.80%. Yearly downtime = 0.001996 x 8760 = 17.5 hours. That misses a 99.9% SLA (budget 8.76h) - you need either higher MTBF or lower MTTR. Halving MTTR to 2h: A = 2000/2002 = 99.9001%, downtime 8.75h - just inside. MTTR is usually the cheaper lever: monitoring, runbooks, and tested restores.

notes.title: Serial vs parallel: the architecture math
notes.body:
Serial (every component must work): A_system = A1 x A2 x ... x An. Availability MULTIPLIES DOWN - three 99.9% components in series give 99.7%. Every dependency you add costs nines.

Parallel (redundant, any one suffices): U_system = U1 x U2 (unavailabilities multiply), so A = 1 - (1-A1)(1-A2). Two 99% components in parallel: U = 0.01 x 0.01 = 0.0001 -> A = 99.99%. Redundancy buys nines fast - IF failures are independent. Shared power, shared switch, or the same bad patch break independence, and the math silently lies.

Worked example (with solution):
Web tier: 2 load-balanced servers, each 99.5% available, sharing one 99.9% switch. What is tier availability?
Parallel servers: U = 0.005 x 0.005 = 0.000025 -> A_servers = 99.9975%.
Series with switch: 0.999975 x 0.999 = 0.998975 = 99.8975%.
The single switch dominates - the 'HA' pair is really a 99.9% system wearing a 99.9975% costume. This is why network redundancy (stacked switches, dual NICs) comes before server redundancy in real designs.

notes.title: SLA budgets, expected value, and p95
notes.body:
An SLA is a downtime BUDGET, not a promise of uptime. 99.9% monthly = 43.8 minutes of allowed outage. Error budgets (from SRE practice) say: spend the budget on risky changes while budget remains; freeze when exhausted. If you burned 40 minutes in week one, week two is change-freeze territory.

Expected value: EV = sum(probability x outcome). A $500 redundant PSU that prevents a 2%-annual-chance 8-hour outage on a system costing $10k/hour in downtime: EV of loss without it = 0.02 x 8 x 10000 = $1,600/yr. The PSU pays for itself 3x over - that is the entire business case for HA in one line.

Percentiles: p50 (median) is the typical experience; p95 is what your unhappiest 5% feel; p99 the worst 1%. Averages hide sins - a 50ms average with a 5s p99 means 1 in 100 users rage-quits. Operators watch p95/p99, not the mean.

Worked example (with solution):
Monthly latencies (ms): 40, 45, 42, 48, 44, 41, 46, 43, 47, 900. Mean = 129.6ms, median = 44.5ms, p95 ~ 900ms.
Report the mean and you claim '130ms typical' - wrong; 9 of 10 users saw ~44ms and one saw 900ms. The p95 tells the true story: the system is fine except for a tail you must investigate (GC pause? noisy neighbor?). Always pair the median with p95.

notes.title: Little's Law: the one equation of every queue
notes.body:
L = lambda x W. L = average number in the system (waiting + being served), lambda = arrival rate (jobs/hour), W = average time each job spends in the system (hours). It holds for ANY queue - helpdesk tickets, print spoolers, TCP connections, backup jobs - regardless of distributions.

Rearrange freely: W = L / lambda (how long will I wait given the line I see?), lambda = L / W (what arrival rate does this backlog imply?).

Worked example (with solution):
The ticket queue holds steady at 40 open tickets; the team closes 10 per day. Average ticket age?
lambda = 10/day, L = 40 -> W = 40/10 = 4 days. A user filing today waits ~4 days on average.
Management wants 1-day turnaround without hiring: need W=1 -> L = lambda x W = 10 x 1 = 10 open tickets max. Either cut arrivals (self-service) or raise service rate - the math allows no third option.

notes.title: Utilization and the hockey-stick curve
notes.body:
Utilization rho = lambda / mu, where mu = service rate (max jobs/hour the server/team can complete). rho < 1 is stable; rho >= 1 means the queue grows forever. The cruelty: wait time doesn't grow linearly - for the simplest queue (M/M/1), average wait = 1/(mu - lambda), which EXPLODES as lambda approaches mu.

At rho = 0.5, waits are mild. At rho = 0.9, waits are ~9x the service time. At rho = 0.99, ~99x. This is why a server at 'only' 90% CPU during a login storm feels dead, and why running any shared resource above ~70-80% sustained utilization is asking for a queueing catastrophe at the first burst.

Worked example (with solution):
A backup server writes at mu = 12 jobs/hour. Arrivals: 10 jobs/hour at night.
rho = 10/12 = 0.833. M/M/1 average time in system W = 1/(mu - lambda) = 1/(12-10) = 0.5 hour per job.
Add two more nightly jobs (lambda = 12): rho = 1.0 - the queue NEVER drains; backlog grows all night. Add just one (lambda=11): W = 1/(12-11) = 1 hour - doubling the wait from one extra job/hour. The knee of the curve is brutal: small arrival increases near saturation cause huge wait increases.

notes.title: Queues you will actually size
notes.body:
Helpdesk staffing: if tickets arrive at 6/hour and each takes 20 min (mu = 3/hour per tech), one tech gives rho = 6/3 = 2 - impossible. Two techs: mu = 6, rho = 1.0 - still unstable (no headroom for bursts). Three techs: mu = 9, rho = 0.67 - healthy with burst headroom. Staffing math is queuing math.

Patching waves: 500 machines, deployment tool does 50/hour (mu), maintenance window 4 hours needs lambda <= 125/hour - fine sequentially, but if all 500 check in at once (thundering herd), the queue is 500 deep and W = 500/50 = 10 hours. Stagger with randomized check-in offsets (splay) to flatten lambda.

Login storms (Monday 9 AM), backup windows, DHCP lease renewals after an outage - every 'everything is slow at the same time' incident is a queue with rho momentarily >= 1. The fix is always one of: raise mu (faster service), lower lambda (stagger/splay), or add parallel servers (more checkout lanes).

Worked example (with solution):
After a power outage, 2000 devices request DHCP simultaneously. Server handles mu = 100 leases/sec. How long until the last device gets an address, and what would cut it in half?
W_last = L/mu = 2000/100 = 20 seconds of pure queue drain (plus service time). To halve: double mu (faster server/two servers = 200/sec -> 10s), or halve L by prestaging (shorter lease backlog). Note the first devices wait ~0s, the last waits ~20s - the queue is unfair by arrival order, which is why 'my laptop got an IP but the printer didn't' after outages.

notes.title: What Big-O means for an admin
notes.body:
Big-O describes how work GROWS with input size n. O(1): constant - a hash table lookup takes the same time for 10 or 10 million entries. O(log n): halving each step - binary search; 1M entries take ~20 steps. O(n): one pass - reading every line once. O(n log n): sorting. O(n^2): nested loops - for each of n users, scan all n computers.

The admin translation: O(n^2) is fine at n=50 (2,500 ops) and a disaster at n=50,000 (2.5 BILLION ops). When a script 'worked in the lab but dies in production', 90% of the time n grew and the complexity was quadratic.

Worked example (with solution):
Script A: foreach ($u in $users) { Get-ADUser $u } with 5,000 users at 0.2s per query = 1,000s (~17 min). Script B: $all = Get-ADUser -Filter * -Properties * once (5s), then hash lookup per user (O(1) each): 5 + 5000x0.0001 = ~5.5s.
Speedup: ~180x. The fix wasn't faster hardware - it was replacing n server round-trips (O(n) with a huge constant) with one bulk fetch plus O(1) lookups. Constants matter too: an O(n) with a 0.2s network constant beats an O(n log n) in-memory sort at small n, but loses as n grows.

notes.title: Spotting n-squared in the wild
notes.body:
The classic admin n-squared: nested iteration over two collections. 'For each computer, check if it's in the stale list' with -contains on an ARRAY is O(n x m): each -contains scans the array. With 10k computers and a 10k stale list, that's 100M comparisons.

Fixes: (1) hash set - put the stale list in a [hashtable] or HashSet, lookups become O(1): total O(n+m). (2) Sort both and merge in one pass: O(n log n). (3) Let the server do it: one LDAP filter instead of client-side loops.

String building is the other trap: $s += $line in a loop copies the whole string each time -> O(n^2) characters copied. Use [System.Text.StringBuilder] or collect in an array and -join once: O(n).

Worked example (with solution):
Compare: array -contains vs hashtable lookup over 20,000 items, 5,000 lookups.
Array: 5,000 lookups x avg 10,000 comparisons = 50M comparisons. Hashtable: 5,000 x ~1 = 5,000.
Measure-Command { 1..5000 | % { $array -contains $_ } } vs Measure-Command { 1..5000 | % { $hash.ContainsKey($_) } } typically shows 100-1000x difference. The lesson: data structure choice IS algorithm choice. An array is a list; a hashtable is an index - and you already know from databases that indexes beat scans.

notes.title: Measuring, sorting, and searching
notes.body:
Never guess - measure: Measure-Command { ... } reports real elapsed time. Compare candidate approaches on production-scale data (or a faithful fraction) before committing. If doubling n quadruples time, you found your n-squared.

Sorting costs O(n log n): Sort-Object on 100k objects is fine; on 10M rows, do it in the database (indexed ORDER BY) not in PowerShell. Searching: linear scan O(n) vs binary search O(log n) - but binary search needs sorted data; if you search once, the sort cost dominates, so just scan. If you search 1,000 times, sort once (O(n log n)) then binary-search (O(log n) each).

Pipeline streaming is O(n) memory-friendly: Get-Content big.log | Where-Object {...} processes line by line. $(Get-Content big.log) first loads everything - same O(n) time but O(n) memory, and on a 10GB log that's the difference between running and crashing.

Worked example (with solution):
Task: find which of 50,000 AD users logged on in the last 30 days (have lastLogonTimestamp).
Bad: foreach user { Get-ADUser $u -Properties lastLogonTimestamp } - 50k queries, ~2.8 hours at 0.2s each.
Good: Get-ADUser -Filter 'lastLogonTimestamp -ge $cutoff' -Properties lastLogonTimestamp - one server-side indexed query, seconds.
Best lesson: the fastest code is the code the server runs for you. Push filters to AD/SQL (WHERE/LDAP filter), keep PowerShell for what servers can't express.

cards.front: ThreatLocker in one sentence (public facts only)
cards.back: Zero Trust endpoint-security company founded 2017 in Orlando, FL by Danny Jenkins, Sami Jenkins, and John Carolan. Public materials describe the team as 'Cyber Heroes' and the mission as a world where organizations operate free from cybercriminal influence.

cards.front: Name the core ThreatLocker platform components.
cards.back: Application Allowlisting, Ringfencing, Storage Control, Elevation Control, Endpoint Network Control, Configuration Management, and Operational Alerts — a default-deny, Zero Trust approach to servers and endpoints.

cards.front: What is 'default-deny' / allowlisting, in one sentence?
cards.back: Instead of trying to recognize every bad file, only explicitly approved applications are allowed to run — everything else is denied by default.

cards.front: What does Ringfencing do, in one sentence?
cards.back: It limits what approved applications are allowed to do — e.g., blocking a trusted app from reaching the internet or touching sensitive files — containing weaponized legitimate software.

cards.back: Easy-to-average difficulty (~2.45/5); many report brief, conversational interviews focused on background, eagerness, and culture fit. cards.back: ThreatLocker hires career-starters in cybersecurity: one July 2026 candidate reported they are 'looking for people starting their career in cybersecurity — as long as you're eager you will be fine.' Eagerness + preparation is the signal.

notes.title: Source discipline: what we know and how we know it
notes.body:
Every company fact in this module comes from one of three public sources: ThreatLocker's public website, ThreatLocker's public job postings, or publicly visible candidate reports (Glassdoor public snippets, fetched 2026-10-07). Full Glassdoor reviews sit behind a sign-in wall — noted as a limit, not bypassed.

What that means in the interview: you can say "I've studied your public materials closely." You cannot claim insider knowledge, employment, certification, or endorsement. If an interviewer asks something you don't know, the honest answer is "I haven't seen that published — here's what I do know about your public approach..."

Grounded fact sheet (public sources only):
- ThreatLocker is a Zero Trust endpoint-security company founded in 2017 in Orlando, Florida, by Danny Jenkins, Sami Jenkins, and John Carolan.
- Public materials describe the team as "Cyber Heroes" and the mission as a world where organizations operate free from cybercriminal influence.
- Core platform components (public site): Application Allowlisting, Ringfencing, Storage Control, Elevation Control, Endpoint Network Control, Configuration Management, Operational Alerts — a default-deny approach to servers and endpoints.
- Candidate reports (Glassdoor public snippets): interview difficulty easy-to-average (~2.45/5); many interviews brief and conversational, focused on background, eagerness, and culture fit; reported questions include "Could you build a virtual machine?", "Why ThreatLocker?", "Why cybersecurity?"; ~18 days average from first interview to offer.
- ThreatLocker publicly described a three-step process for a Senior Technical Support Specialist role: (1) technical phone interview, (2) product demo presentation back to the team, (3) onsite hands-on troubleshooting session. The IT Infrastructure Specialist loop may differ — prepare for all three.
- Public postings describe a background check and drug/substance screening after a conditional offer.
- Culture signals (public snippets): ~3.3/5 overall; in-office culture emphasized, no remote work; fast-paced, high-expectation environment; leadership praised in positive reviews.

notes.title: The 60-second company answer — worked example
notes.body:
When they ask "What do you know about ThreatLocker?" they are scoring three things: did you do the work, can you explain their model in your own words, and do you sound like a believer without sounding like a fanboy. Structure: company → approach → products → mission. Sixty seconds, no notes.

Worked example — say it aloud and time it:
> "ThreatLocker is a Zero Trust endpoint security company founded in 2017 in Orlando. Their whole platform is built on default-deny: instead of trying to recognize every piece of malware, Application Allowlisting means only explicitly approved software is allowed to run — everything else is denied by default. Then Ringfencing limits what even approved applications are allowed to do, so a trusted app can't be weaponized to reach the internet or touch sensitive files. Around that core they've built Storage Control, Elevation Control, Endpoint Network Control, Configuration Management, and Operational Alerts. The mission, in their words, is a world where organizations operate free from cybercriminal influence — and honestly, default-deny is the direction I believe endpoint security has to go, which is why I'm here."

Why this works: every claim is a public fact. It shows you understand the *model*, not just the product list. It ends with conviction, not flattery. Practice until it flows in your own words — never recite it verbatim or you'll sound rehearsed.

notes.title: Allowlisting: the core product, explained three ways
notes.body:
You must be able to explain allowlisting at three altitudes. Worked examples:

**To a fellow technician (precise):** "Allowlisting inverts the endpoint security model. Instead of maintaining signatures of known-bad files — an infinite, losing list — the agent enforces a policy of known-good executables. Anything not on the approved list is denied execution by default. Updates and new software go through an approval workflow, so the environment stays in a known-good state."

**To a non-technical manager (analogy):** "Think of it as a guest list instead of a most-wanted list. A bouncer with a most-wanted list has to recognize every criminal in the world. A bouncer with a guest list just checks whether you're on it. Allowlisting is the guest list for software."

**In one sentence (the interview answer):** "Only explicitly approved applications are allowed to run — everything else is denied by default."

Common follow-up: "Doesn't that break everything when users need new software?" Strong answer: "That's what the approval workflow and learning modes are for — the platform catalogs what's in the environment and admins approve through a request process, so legitimate software gets in quickly while unknown executables stay blocked. It's a process change as much as a technology change, and that's the honest trade-off.

notes.title: Ringfencing and the control suite — one-liners plus a worked scenario
notes.body:
One-sentence briefs for each public component. Memorize these cold:
- **Ringfencing:** limits what approved applications are allowed to *do* — e.g., blocking a trusted app from reaching the internet or touching sensitive files — containing weaponized legitimate software.
- **Storage Control:** governs which applications may write to protected storage locations, blocking ransomware-style mass encryption by untrusted processes.
- **Elevation Control:** governs when applications may run with elevated privileges, so users operate as standard accounts and elevation is granted deliberately.
- **Endpoint Network Control:** controls what the endpoint itself may reach on the network.
- **Configuration Management:** keeps endpoint configuration in a desired, auditable state.
- **Operational Alerts:** surfaces blocked/attempted actions so the team sees what the controls stopped.

Worked scenario — "Walk me through how Ringfencing stops an attack":
> "Say a user opens a malicious document and the PDF reader has a zero-day. The reader is an approved application, so allowlisting lets it run. But Ringfencing policy says the reader may not launch child processes or reach the internet. The exploit fires, tries to download a payload — denied. Tries to encrypt the documents folder — Storage Control denies the write. The attempt is logged and the team gets an Operational Alert. Three layers, one incident, zero damage — and none of it required recognizing the malware."

That scenario is the *concept* of the platform as publicly described — present it as your understanding of the model, not as insider product knowledge.

notes.title: What candidates report: process, culture, and the limits of what we know
notes.body:
Public candidate reports (Glassdoor public snippets, fetched 2026-10-07) paint a consistent picture — and you must know both the picture and its limits.

**What multiple candidates report:**
- Difficulty skews easy-to-average (~2.45/5). Many describe brief, conversational interviews focused on background, eagerness, and culture fit rather than deep technical grilling.
- Frequently reported questions: "Could you build a virtual machine?", "Why ThreatLocker?", "Why cybersecurity?", "Tell me about yourself."
- One July 2026 candidate reported the hiring signal directly: they are "looking for people starting their career in cybersecurity — as long as you're eager you will be fine." Eagerness + preparation is the signal.
- Average ~18 days from first interview to offer (Glassdoor aggregate).
- Post-offer: public postings describe a background check and drug/substance screening after a conditional offer.
- Culture (public snippets): ~3.3/5 overall; in-office culture with no remote work; fast-paced, high-expectation; leadership praised in positive reviews.

**The limits — say these to yourself, not necessarily aloud:**
- These are aggregates and snippets, not a complete picture. Your loop may differ.
- The three-step process (phone → demo → onsite troubleshooting) was described for a *Senior Technical Support Specialist* role, not IT Infrastructure Specialist. Prepare for all formats anyway — that's the point of FT04.
- Never cite Glassdoor in the interview ("I read on Glassdoor that..."). Use the knowledge silently: be ready for conversational culture-fit questions, have the VM answer ready, lead with eagerness.

**Worked example — using this knowledge without citing it:**
Interviewer: "So why us?" Weak answer: "I saw the reviews are good." Strong answer: "Because your default-deny approach is the direction I believe endpoint security has to go, and I want to build my infrastructure career inside a company whose product philosophy I can defend. I enrolled in your Zero Trust bootcamp on September 30th — I'm not casually interested, I'm invested." (See FT02-B01.)

notes.title: The independent-prep line: exact phrases to use and avoid
notes.body:
You are a knowledgeable independent candidate. Every sentence you say must keep that line. Worked pairs — the wrong version, then the right version:

❌ "As a ThreatLocker-certified engineer..." → ✅ "I've studied your public platform materials closely as an independent candidate..."
❌ "My insider contact told me your interview process is..." → ✅ "From your public postings and candidate reports, I understand the process may include... I've prepared for each format."
❌ "I completed your bootcamp." → ✅ "I enrolled in the Zero Trust bootcamp on September 30th and have been working through the material since."
❌ "I was basically promised this role." → ✅ (never say anything like this; no hiring promise exists or is implied)
❌ "I know exactly how your console works." → ✅ "My understanding of the model from your public materials is... — I'd love to learn the console itself on the job."

The principle: deep knowledge of *public* material + explicit honesty about the boundary. Interviewers at a security company are professionally paranoid about exaggeration — the candidate who says "here's what I know, here's what I don't" earns trust faster than the one who bluffs.

Drill this with FT01-D3 until the right phrasing is automatic.

notes.title: Visual: the default-deny model as a diagram
notes.body:
Study this until you can redraw it from memory — then do exactly that on the whiteboard if they ask "how does it all fit together?"

```
                    ┌─────────────────────────────────┐
                    │        UNTRUSTED BY DEFAULT      │
                    │   every executable, every user,  │
                    │   every network flow             │
                    └───────────────┬─────────────────┘
                                    │ policy decision
                    ┌───────────────▼─────────────────┐
                    │      ALLOWLISTING (what runs)    │
                    │  known-good hash? signed by     │
                    │  trusted publisher? → APPROVED  │
                    │  otherwise → DENIED by default  │
                    └───────────────┬─────────────────┘
                                    │ approved apps only
              ┌─────────────────────▼─────────────────────┐
              │        RINGFENCING (what it may do)        │
              │  internet access?  ──► policy decides     │
              │  sensitive files?  ──► policy decides     │
              │  child processes?  ──► policy decides     │
              │  even trusted apps get boundaries         │
              └─────────────────────┬─────────────────────┘
                                    │
        ┌───────────────────────────┼───────────────────────────┐
        │                           │                           │
┌───────▼────────┐       ┌──────────▼─────────┐       ┌─────────▼────────┐
│ STORAGE CTRL   │       │ ELEVATION CTRL     │       │ NETWORK CTRL     │
│ which apps may │       │ when apps may run  │       │ what endpoints   │
│ write where    │       │ elevated           │       │ may reach         │
└───────┬────────┘       └──────────┬─────────┘       └────────┬─────────┘
        │                           │                          │
        └───────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────┘
                                    ▼
                    ┌───────────────────────────────┐
                    │ CONFIG MGMT: desired state,    │
                    │ auditable                     │
                    │ OPERATIONAL ALERTS: every     │
                    │ blocked attempt is visible    │
                    └───────────────────────────────┘
```

Read it top-down in the interview: "Everything starts untrusted. Allowlisting decides what runs. Ringfencing decides what the approved apps may do. The control suite governs storage, elevation, and network. Configuration management keeps it auditable, and operational alerts make every blocked attempt visible."

The one-line version: **deny by default, approve explicitly, constrain continuously, alert on everything.** If you can say that sentence and draw this diagram, you understand their model better than 90% of candidates.

notes.title: How to use this bank: the 6-day method
notes.body:
Sixty questions across eight categories. Nine are publicly reported by ThreatLocker candidates (marked 'reported by candidates'); the rest are likely probes authored for this IT Infrastructure Specialist role (marked 'likely'). The model answers are starting points — rebuild each in your own words and anchor it to something you have actually done.

The method, day by day:
- **Days 1–2 (FT track day 2):** Work one category per day aloud. 90 seconds per answer, phone recording on. Behavioral first — those are the reported questions and the highest-probability asks.
- **Day 3:** Random sampling. Have someone (or a random-number generator) pick 15 questions across categories. No warm-up, no cherry-picking.
- **Day 4 (mock day):** FT04 pulls 8 from this bank under timed conditions.
- **Day 5:** Weak-question drill — only the questions you scored 0–1 on. Re-answer until every one is a 2 or 3.

Rules that never bend: never memorize model answers word-for-word — interviewers detect recitation instantly and it reads as dishonest. Every technical answer gets paired with evidence from your real history (homelab, founder work, bootcamp). If an interviewer asks where you prepared, say "public candidate reports and your public materials" — never claim insider knowledge.

notes.title: The 90-second answer architecture — worked example
notes.body:
Every technical answer follows the same skeleton: **verdict → method → evidence → close**. Ninety seconds is roughly 200 words aloud. Worked example with FT02-N01 ("A user can't reach the internet but can reach local servers"):

> **Verdict (10s):** "Local works, so the local stack is fine — this is a gateway, DNS, or upstream problem."
> **Method (45s):** "I'd isolate it in order: ping the default gateway first — if that fails, it's the gateway or the local route. Then ping 8.8.8.8: if IPs work but names don't, it's DNS — check the resolver config and try nslookup. If neither works past the gateway, it's the gateway itself or upstream — check the gateway's status and the WAN link."
> **Evidence (20s):** "I've run exactly this triage in my homelab when a VM lost external access after a virtual-switch change — turned out to be the gateway assignment on the new switch."
> **Close (10s):** "Layered, outside-in, and I verify each layer before moving up."

Why it scores: the interviewer hears a *method*, not just an answer. The evidence line is short and real. The whole thing fits in 90 seconds. Now do the same for FT02-W02 (GPO not applying): verdict "scope issue until proven otherwise" → method "gpresult, OU link, filtering, inheritance, replication" → evidence "homelab GPO for workstation baselines" → close.

notes.title: Handling reported questions — worked example
notes.body:
The nine reported questions are your highest-probability asks. They skew conversational — which means most candidates under-prepare them and ramble. Worked example with FT02-B03 ("Could you build a virtual machine?"):

Weak answer: "Yeah, I've built VMs before." (Scores 1/3 — vague, no evidence.)
Strong answer (90 seconds):
> "Yes — and I can walk you through it. Enable the Hyper-V role, create an external virtual switch for network access, then create the VM: Generation 2 for a modern OS, assign vCPUs and RAM with headroom for the workload, attach a dynamically expanding VHDX sized for it, mount the ISO, install the OS, install integration services, apply my baseline configuration, and take a checkpoint before any changes. I've done this repeatedly in my homelab — I can whiteboard the whole flow right now if you'd like."

The structure: **yes + ordered steps + specific nouns (Hyper-V, Gen2, VHDX) + offer to demonstrate**. The offer to whiteboard is the power move — it converts a verbal question into a practical demonstration, and interviewers remember it.

Do the same treatment for each reported question: FT02-B01 (why ThreatLocker → conviction + bootcamp date), FT02-B04 (endpoint security → show you studied THEIR model), FT02-B05 (hardest homelab problem → the RAID 0 migration, lesson-first).

notes.title: Anchoring to real evidence — worked example
notes.body:
A correct answer with no evidence scores 2/3. A correct answer anchored to something you've done scores 3/3. The transformation, worked example with FT02-E03 (patching without breaking users):

Generic (2/3): "Ringed rollouts: pilot group first, then broad deployment with deadlines and notifications, maintenance windows for servers, expedited rings for zero-days, and a rollback plan."

Anchored (3/3): "Ringed rollouts: pilot group first, then broad deployment with deadlines and user notifications. I learned the discipline running my own infrastructure — when I maintain my homelab hosts, I patch one node, validate services, then roll to the rest, with a snapshot before each ring. Same principle at fleet scale: expedited ring for critical zero-days, deferrals with hard deadlines for workstations, and a rollback plan before any fleet-wide push."

The anchor doesn't have to be enterprise — it has to be *real*. Your evidence inventory: homelab builds and migrations, founder/DevSecOps production operations, bootcamp enrollment, the Oct 7 prep marathon. Map every FT02 technical question to at least one inventory item before mock day.

notes.title: Recitation vs fluency: what interviewers detect
notes.body:
Interviewers — especially at a security company — are trained to detect memorization. The tells: identical phrasing across answers, unnatural pacing, eyes defocusing mid-answer, collapse when interrupted with a follow-up. A memorized answer that gets a follow-up question dies; an *understood* answer adapts.

Worked example — the follow-up test. You deliver FT02-Z01 ("What is Zero Trust?") fluently: "Never trust, always verify — every access request authenticated, authorized, continuously re-evaluated." The interviewer follows up: "Okay, so how does that change how you'd design our office network?" The reciter freezes or repeats the definition. The fluent candidate reasons aloud: "I'd assume breach from the start — micro-segment the network so departments are isolated zones, put identity at the center with MFA and conditional access, remove implicit trust for anything inside the perimeter, and make every cross-segment connection an explicit, logged decision."

Train for follow-ups, not just questions: after every bank answer, ask yourself "why?" and "how would you apply that here?" twice. That's the FT04 branching-scenario muscle.

notes.title: Provenance honesty in the room
notes.body:
If an interviewer asks where you prepared — or if a question clearly comes from candidate reports — the honest framing is: "From your public materials and public candidate reports." Never imply insider knowledge. Never say "I heard your interviews are easy." Never reference Glassdoor by name.

Worked example — the trap and the recovery. Interviewer: "You seem well-prepared for our process. How did you know what to expect?" Weak: "I read all about it online." Strong: "I studied your public platform materials closely, and I prepared for the formats you've publicly described — technical conversation, a demo-style presentation, and hands-on troubleshooting — because I'd rather be over-prepared for your format than surprised by it."

Notice what the strong answer does: it demonstrates knowledge of the three-step structure *without* claiming it applies to this loop, and it frames preparation as respect for their time. That's the independent-prep line held under pressure.

objectives: Answer any of the 60 questions aloud, in under 90 seconds, without notes.
Distinguish publicly reported ThreatLocker interview questions from likely probes — and nail both.
Deliver model answers in your own words; never recite verbatim.
Pair every technical answer with evidence from your real history.

provenanceKey.reported by candidates: Publicly reported by ThreatLocker interview candidates on Glassdoor (publicly visible content, fetched 2026-10-07; corroborated by the source-sweep worker's interview-experience mining). Full reviews sit behind a sign-in wall — noted as a limit, not bypassed. Nine bank items carry this mark and together cover ten distinct reported questions (the two 'why ThreatLocker' variants are merged into FT02-B01).
provenanceKey.likely: Authored for this IT Infrastructure Specialist role based on the certification domains and the two real ThreatLocker IT postings mined for the JD matrix. Not reported questions.

questions.question: Why do you want to work at ThreatLocker?
questions.sourceNote: Reported by multiple Orlando candidates on Glassdoor (publicly visible, fetched 2026-10-07).
questions.modelAnswer: Because ThreatLocker's default-deny, Zero Trust approach is the direction I believe endpoint security has to go, and I want to build my infrastructure career inside a company whose product philosophy I can defend. I've spent the last months studying your public platform materials and enrolled in the Zero Trust bootcamp on September 30th — I'm not casually interested, I'm invested.
talkingPoints: Bootcamp enrollment Sept 30 as proof of initiative

questions.question: Why did you choose cybersecurity / IT infrastructure?
questions.sourceNote: Reported by a July 2026 Orlando candidate on Glassdoor.
questions.modelAnswer: I started as a builder — homelabs, self-hosted infrastructure, DevSecOps work at my own company — and every system I built taught me the same lesson: the infrastructure decisions ARE the security decisions. I want to do that work where it matters most, inside a security company.

questions.question: Could you build a virtual machine?
questions.sourceNote: Reported by a hired Cyber Hero in Orlando on Glassdoor. Expect a hands-on follow-up.
questions.modelAnswer: Yes — and I can walk you through it: choose the hypervisor, size vCPU/RAM/storage for the workload, create the virtual switch, attach the ISO, install the OS, apply baselines, snapshot before changes. I've done this repeatedly in my homelab with Hyper-V.
talkingPoints: Answer yes with the concrete steps
Offer to whiteboard it on the spot

questions.question: What do you know about endpoint security?
questions.sourceNote: Reported for a ThreatLocker Application Technician interview on Glassdoor.
questions.modelAnswer: Endpoint security is the last line of defense on the device itself: controlling what runs, what it can do, and what leaves the machine. The strongest model I've studied is default-deny — allowlisting plus ringfencing so even trusted apps can't be weaponized — backed by baselines, patching, and EDR telemetry for what slips through.

questions.question: What is the most technically difficult problem you've run into in your homelab?
questions.sourceNote: Reported for a ThreatLocker Application Technician interview — asked right after the candidate described their homelab.
questions.modelAnswer: Migrating my live data to a RAID 0 array while keeping services up. The challenge was sequencing: verify backups, build the array, migrate in stages with checksums, and validate every service after cutover. It taught me that infrastructure work is really change-management work — the plan matters more than the commands.

questions.question: How do you respond to a frustrated or angry customer?
questions.sourceNote: Reported for a ThreatLocker Application Technician interview on Glassdoor.
questions.modelAnswer: First I de-escalate: acknowledge the impact, not the tone. Then I take ownership of the next step with a clear ETA, communicate proactively until it's resolved, and document what happened so it doesn't recur. Frustration usually means they feel unheard — so I make sure they feel heard and then I fix it.

questions.question: Tell me about a time you had a problem with a coworker and how you resolved it.
questions.sourceNote: Reported for a ThreatLocker Application Technician interview on Glassdoor.
questions.modelAnswer: As a founder I've mostly managed myself, so I'll answer with how I handle disagreement: I separate the technical question from the personal one, state my reasoning with evidence, listen for what I'm missing, and converge on the option with the best trade-offs — then commit fully once decided. Disagree-and-commit beats silent resentment.

questions.question: Tell me about yourself and your goals.
questions.sourceNote: Reported on Glassdoor's ThreatLocker interview page (publicly visible, fetched 2026-10-07); corroborated by the source-sweep worker's interview-experience mining.
questions.modelAnswer: I'm a DevSecOps and full-stack builder — founder of Interstitium Labs — with deep homelab infrastructure experience: Windows Server, Active Directory, Hyper-V virtualization, networking, PowerShell automation, and endpoint hardening. I enrolled in ThreatLocker's Zero Trust bootcamp on September 30th and have spent the last week in focused interview preparation. My goal: become a trusted infrastructure specialist here and earn senior-level capability fast.
talkingPoints: Ends with the goal, not just history

questions.question: Are you comfortable with rejection?
questions.sourceNote: Reported on Glassdoor; context suggests a sales-track interview — included for completeness.
questions.modelAnswer: In infrastructure, 'rejection' looks like a change request being denied or a design being challenged — and I'm comfortable with both, because a no with a reason makes the system better. I separate the decision from my ego and ask what would make it a yes.

questions.question: Tell me about a time you failed.
questions.sourceNote: Likely behavioral probe for resilience and honesty.
questions.modelAnswer: Early in a homelab migration I skipped the verification step on a backup and discovered mid-cutover it was incomplete. I stopped, rebuilt the backup properly, and finished the migration a day late but with zero data loss. Now verification is a non-negotiable gate in every plan I write — I even built it into my runbook template.
talkingPoints: Real pattern from his migration work

questions.question: Where do you see yourself in two years?
questions.sourceNote: Likely closing question; tests ambition vs. flight risk.
questions.modelAnswer: A trusted infrastructure specialist here — the person the team hands the hard escalations to — with certifications to match: Security+, AZ-800, AZ-801. I want depth in this stack and this company, not a quick hop.

questions.question: Why should we hire you over a more experienced candidate?
questions.sourceNote: Likely for a junior candidate; turn inexperience into an asset.
questions.modelAnswer: Experience I can't fake, so I won't. What I offer: I learn systems end-to-end instead of memorizing steps, I document everything, I prepare obsessively — this interview is the proof — and I have no bad habits to unlearn. You'd be hiring trajectory, not just history.

questions.question: Walk me through promoting a new domain controller.
questions.sourceNote: Core AZ-800/AD DS competency for the role.
questions.modelAnswer: Install the AD DS role, promote with dcpromo-equivalent wizard or Install-ADDSDomainController, verify DNS integration, check replication with repadmin, confirm SYSVOL replication, and validate FSMO placement. Then monitor event logs for the first 24 hours.

questions.question: A GPO isn't applying to a user. How do you troubleshoot?
questions.modelAnswer: Check scope: is the user/computer in the linked OU? Run gpresult /r to see what's applied and denied. Check link order, Enforced/Block Inheritance, security filtering, WMI filters, and replication — then gpupdate /force and re-check. Fix the scope issue, don't just re-link randomly.

questions.question: Explain OU design best practices.
questions.modelAnswer: Design OUs around delegation and policy needs — not the org chart alone. Keep the structure shallow, separate users from computers where policies differ, use security groups for permissions rather than stuffing OUs, and document the design rationale so the next admin understands it.

questions.question: How would you reset a user's password securely and communicate it?
questions.modelAnswer: Verify identity first — never reset on an unverified request. Reset in ADUC or PowerShell, set 'must change at next logon' where policy requires, and deliver the temporary credential through a separate verified channel, never in the same message as the request.

questions.question: What is the difference between share and NTFS permissions?
questions.sourceNote: High-frequency interview question; tests layered access understanding.
questions.modelAnswer: Share permissions gate network access to the share; NTFS permissions gate the files themselves. Effective access is the MOST restrictive combination of the two. Best practice: set share to Everyone/Full Control and manage precisely with NTFS.

questions.question: How do you handle a suspected compromised domain account?
questions.modelAnswer: Contain first: disable or force-reset the account, revoke sessions, check logons in the security event log for lateral movement. Then investigate scope before re-enabling — and review how it was compromised so the gap gets closed, not just the symptom.

questions.question: Explain DHCP failover or scope design for a branch office.
questions.modelAnswer: Size the scope with headroom, set appropriate lease durations — shorter for guest/BYOD, longer for stable desktops — configure reservations for printers and infrastructure, and use DHCP failover or a second server so one failure doesn't take down addressing.

questions.question: What would you check if replication between domain controllers is failing?
questions.modelAnswer: Start with the basics: network connectivity and DNS — replication lives or dies on name resolution. Then check time sync, repadmin /showrepl for errors, event logs, and firewall ports. Most replication failures are DNS or time, not AD itself.

questions.question: A user can't reach the internet but can reach local servers. Walk me through it.
questions.modelAnswer: Local works, so L1/L2 and the local stack are fine. Check the default gateway, then DNS — ping 8.8.8.8 to separate routing from name resolution. If IPs work but names don't, it's DNS; if neither works past the gateway, it's the gateway or upstream. Verify each layer before moving up.
talkingPoints: Isolate: gateway vs DNS vs upstream

questions.question: Explain subnetting to a non-technical manager.
questions.sourceNote: Tests communication skill, not just knowledge.
questions.modelAnswer: Subnetting is dividing one big network into smaller neighborhoods. Each neighborhood gets its own address range, which keeps broadcast noise contained, lets us apply different security rules per area, and makes problems easier to locate. A /24 gives about 250 usable addresses — one neighborhood.

questions.question: What is a VLAN and why would you use one?
questions.modelAnswer: A VLAN logically segments one physical switch into multiple broadcast domains. You'd use them to separate traffic types — workstations, servers, guests, VoIP — so a broadcast storm or compromise in one area doesn't take down the others, without buying separate switches.

questions.question: How does DNS resolution actually work, step by step?
questions.sourceNote: Tests depth on a fundamental service.
questions.modelAnswer: The client asks its configured resolver; the resolver checks cache, then walks the hierarchy — root, TLD, authoritative — caching at each level, and returns the answer with a TTL. Failures at each step have distinct signatures, which is why understanding the chain matters for troubleshooting.

questions.question: What would you look at first for intermittent network drops affecting one workstation?
questions.modelAnswer: Physical layer first: cable, port, NIC — swap the patch cable and try another switch port. Then check for IP conflicts, duplex mismatch, and the workstation's event logs. Single-host intermittent issues are usually physical or configuration, not infrastructure-wide.

questions.question: Explain the difference between TCP and UDP and when you'd choose each.
questions.modelAnswer: TCP is connection-oriented with delivery guarantees — file transfers, web, email. UDP is fire-and-forget with low overhead — DNS queries, streaming, VoIP. You choose TCP when correctness matters and UDP when speed matters more than perfect delivery.

questions.question: What is NAT and why does it still matter?
questions.modelAnswer: NAT translates private internal addresses to public ones at the network edge, which conserved IPv4 space and adds a layer of obscurity — internal addresses aren't directly reachable. It matters because nearly every office network still depends on it, even as IPv6 grows.

questions.question: How would you secure a small office wireless network?
questions.modelAnswer: WPA3 or WPA2-Enterprise, a strong unique admin password, guest network isolated on its own VLAN, disable WPS, keep firmware updated, and place APs based on a real survey — not just plugged in where convenient. Then document the configuration.

questions.question: Walk me through creating a Hyper-V virtual machine.
questions.sourceNote: Directly extends the reported 'Could you build a virtual machine?' question.
questions.modelAnswer: Enable the Hyper-V role, create a virtual switch — external for network access — then create the VM: Generation 2 for modern OS, assign vCPUs and RAM with headroom, attach a dynamically expanding VHDX sized for the workload, mount the ISO, install the OS, install integration services, apply baselines, and take a checkpoint before any changes.

questions.question: What is the difference between a VM and a container?
questions.modelAnswer: A VM virtualizes hardware and runs a full guest OS — strong isolation, heavier. A container shares the host OS kernel and isolates at the process level — lighter and faster to start, but with a shared kernel. You pick VMs for strong isolation and heterogeneous OS needs, containers for dense, portable microservices.

questions.question: When would you use a checkpoint versus a backup?
questions.modelAnswer: Checkpoints are for short-term rollback before a change — patching, config edits — and live on the same storage as the VM. Backups are for real recovery: off-host, tested restores, ransomware scenarios. A checkpoint is not a backup, and I'd never let anyone treat it as one.

questions.question: How do you decide how much RAM and CPU to give a VM?
questions.modelAnswer: Start from the workload's measured needs, not guesses — monitor the physical equivalent or pilot. Allocate with modest headroom, enable Dynamic Memory where appropriate, and watch host-level contention. Overprovisioning everything is just as bad as underprovisioning: it wastes resources and hides real bottlenecks.

questions.question: What is a virtual switch and what are the types?
questions.modelAnswer: A virtual switch connects VMs to each other and to networks in software. External binds to a physical NIC for outside access; internal allows VM-to-host communication; private is VM-to-VM only. Choosing the wrong type is a classic 'VM has no network' root cause.

questions.question: How would you troubleshoot a VM that won't boot?
questions.modelAnswer: Check the VM state and Hyper-V event logs first, then walk the boot chain: virtual hardware present, ISO/VHDX attached and valid, boot order, Generation mismatch with the OS, and integration services. If the VHDX is corrupt, that's when the backup — not the checkpoint — conversation starts.

questions.question: How would you harden a new Windows workstation before deployment?
questions.modelAnswer: Start from a known-good image or baseline: patch fully, remove bloatware, enforce BitLocker, configure Defender policies, apply least-privilege local accounts, disable unneeded services, set a standard firewall profile, enroll in management, and document the baseline so drift is detectable.

questions.question: What is least privilege and how do you apply it day-to-day?
questions.modelAnswer: Users get only the access their job requires — no local admin for daily work, separate admin accounts for elevation, and regular reviews to prune what's stale. Day-to-day it means saying no to broad access requests and offering the narrow alternative that still unblocks the work.

questions.question: How do you handle patching without breaking users' work?
questions.modelAnswer: Ringed rollouts: pilot group first, then broad deployment with deadlines and user notifications. Maintenance windows for servers, deferrals with hard deadlines for workstations, and expedited rings for critical zero-days. And a rollback plan before any fleet-wide push.

questions.question: What would you do if EDR flags a workstation?
questions.modelAnswer: Don't ignore it and don't nuke it immediately: isolate the host from the network while preserving state, review the alert context and timeline, escalate per the IR plan with severity, and let forensics determine scope before reimaging. Speed matters, but so does evidence.

questions.question: Explain BitLocker and when you'd enforce it.
questions.modelAnswer: BitLocker is full-disk encryption that protects data if a device is lost or stolen. I'd enforce it on every portable device via policy, escrow recovery keys centrally so a forgotten PIN doesn't mean data loss, and verify compliance rather than assuming it.

questions.question: How do you keep track of which devices are compliant?
questions.modelAnswer: Compliance policies define the healthy state — OS version, encryption, patch level — and the management platform reports compliance continuously. I watch trends, not just individual failures: a spike in noncompliance usually means a broken ring, a bad profile, or fleet drift, and that's the real problem to fix.

questions.question: What is application allowlisting and why does it matter here?
questions.sourceNote: Directly connects his prep to ThreatLocker's model.
questions.modelAnswer: Allowlisting flips the security model: instead of trying to recognize every bad file, only explicitly approved applications may run. It's ThreatLocker's core approach, and it matters because it stops unknown threats — zero-days, novel ransomware — that signature-based tools miss by definition.

questions.question: How would you find all disabled AD user accounts with PowerShell?
questions.modelAnswer: Get-ADUser with a filter on Enabled -eq $false, selecting name, last logon, and distinguished name, exported to CSV for review. One line for the query, but I'd wrap it in a script with logging if it becomes a recurring audit.

questions.question: A script works on your machine but fails on a server. What do you check?
questions.modelAnswer: Execution policy, PowerShell version and module availability, permissions of the running account, and WinRM configuration for remoting. 'Works on my machine' failures are almost always environmental — so I check the environment systematically instead of rewriting the script.

questions.question: How do you safely test a script that modifies production systems?
questions.modelAnswer: WhatIf first, then a lab or pilot group, then production with logging and a rollback plan. Destructive cmdlets get -Confirm behavior reviewed and explicit safeguards. No script touches production untested — that's a rule, not a preference.

questions.question: How would you check disk space across all servers quickly?
questions.modelAnswer: A loop over the server list with Get-CimInstance for Win32_LogicalDisk via CIM sessions, collecting free space and percent free into a report, alerting under threshold. Ten minutes to write, saves hours of manual checking forever.

questions.question: Explain PowerShell remoting and its security considerations.
questions.modelAnswer: PowerShell remoting executes commands on remote machines over WinRM — the backbone of managing Server Core and fleets. Secure it with HTTPS listeners or constrained endpoints, JEA for least-privilege delegation, and never enable unencrypted basic auth across the network.

questions.question: How do you parse a large log file for errors efficiently?
questions.modelAnswer: Select-String with patterns for the error signatures, filtering by timestamp to narrow the window, and exporting matches with context lines. For recurring hunts, I'd parameterize it into a reusable function rather than retyping the pipeline every incident.

questions.question: What is the pipeline and why does it matter?
questions.modelAnswer: The pipeline passes rich .NET objects — not just text — between cmdlets, so you filter, sort, and act on structured data without parsing strings. It matters because it makes one-liners composable: get the objects, filter to the problem set, take action, all in one auditable line.

questions.question: What is Zero Trust in plain language?
questions.modelAnswer: Never trust, always verify. No device or user gets implicit trust just for being inside the network — every access request is authenticated, authorized against policy, and continuously re-evaluated based on identity, device health, and context.

questions.question: How does Zero Trust change traditional network security?
questions.modelAnswer: Traditional security built a hard perimeter with a soft interior — once inside, you were trusted. Zero Trust assumes breach, removes that implicit trust, and pushes enforcement to identity and every resource: micro-segmentation, least privilege, and continuous verification replace the castle-and-moat.

questions.question: What role does identity play in Zero Trust?
questions.modelAnswer: Identity becomes the control plane — the new perimeter. Every decision starts with who is requesting, from what device, in what context. That's why MFA, conditional access, and privileged identity management aren't extras; they're the foundation everything else builds on.

questions.question: Give a concrete example of least privilege in infrastructure work.
questions.modelAnswer: A helpdesk tech gets rights to reset passwords and unlock accounts — not domain admin. A backup service account can read the volumes it protects but can't log on interactively. I review these quarterly, because privilege creeps and every standing privilege is a future incident.

questions.question: How does micro-segmentation limit damage?
questions.modelAnswer: By splitting the network into small isolated zones with explicit allow rules between them, a compromise in one segment can't freely move laterally. The attacker wins one room, not the building — and every cross-segment attempt generates a detectable event.

questions.question: How would you explain ThreatLocker's approach to a skeptical sysadmin?
questions.sourceNote: Tests ability to advocate the company's model credibly.
questions.modelAnswer: I'd say: you already know signature-based tools miss novel threats — you've lived it. Default-deny flips the problem: instead of recognizing infinite bad, you approve finite good. Ringfencing then limits what even approved apps can do. It's the strictest version of least privilege, applied to software execution itself.

questions.question: Walk me through your incident response process.
questions.modelAnswer: Preparation, detection and analysis, containment, eradication, recovery, lessons learned. In practice: contain first to stop the bleeding — isolate hosts, disable accounts — preserve evidence, determine scope before declaring victory, recover in the right order with identity first, then write the after-action so it doesn't repeat.

questions.question: You suspect ransomware on a file server. First three actions?
questions.modelAnswer: One: isolate the server from the network immediately to stop spread. Two: alert per the IR plan and begin scoping — which shares, which accounts. Three: preserve evidence and verify clean backups exist before any recovery talk. Speed on containment, discipline on everything after.

questions.question: How do you determine the scope of a compromise?
questions.modelAnswer: Start from the initial indicator and expand: authentication logs for the affected accounts, network connections from the host, persistence mechanisms, and timeline correlation across sources. Scope is a question you answer with evidence, not assumptions — and you keep expanding until the evidence stops, not until you're tired.

questions.question: When do you escalate versus handle it yourself?
questions.modelAnswer: I handle what's in my scope and escalate when: the blast radius exceeds my authority, I see signs of active adversary presence, or I'm stuck past a reasonable timebox with no progress. Escalation isn't failure — late escalation is. I'd rather escalate early with a clean handoff than heroically fail alone.

questions.question: What goes into a good after-action report?
questions.modelAnswer: Timeline of what happened, root cause, what worked and what didn't in the response, and concrete action items with owners and dates. Blameless on people, ruthless on gaps. The report isn't done until the action items are tracked somewhere they'll actually get finished.

questions.question: How do you communicate during an active incident?
questions.modelAnswer: One clear channel, regular updates even when there's nothing new — 'still investigating, next update at :30' beats silence. Technical detail for the response team, impact and ETA for stakeholders, no speculation stated as fact. And everything important written down, because memory lies during incidents.

quiz.q: An interviewer asks a 'reported' question: 'Could you build a virtual machine?' What is the winning structure?
choices: Yes + concrete ordered steps + offer to whiteboard it
Talk about your favorite hypervisor's history
quiz.explain: Yes, then prove it with steps, then offer to demonstrate — confidence plus evidence.

quiz.q: How should you handle the 'likely' questions differently from the 'reported' ones?
choices: Prepare both identically: 90-second answers anchored to real experience
quiz.explain: Provenance tells you what to expect, not what to skip — both get the same rigorous preparation.

quiz.q: You answer a technical question correctly but with zero evidence from your history. What score and why?
choices: 2/3 — correct but unanchored; evidence is what earns the third point
quiz.explain: The bank's rubric: 2 = correct, 3 = correct + evidence. Map every question to your inventory.

quiz.q: An interviewer interrupts your memorized Zero Trust answer with 'how would you apply that to our office network?' What distinguishes the fluent candidate?
choices: Reasoning aloud from the model: assume breach, micro-segment, identity-centered, explicit cross-segment decisions
quiz.explain: Fluency = reasoning from the model under follow-up pressure. Train 'why?' x2 after every answer.

quiz.q: What is the correct provenance framing if asked where you prepared?
choices: 'From your public materials and public candidate reports' — never claim insider knowledge
quiz.explain: Public-materials framing; never name Glassdoor, never imply insider access.

quiz.q: For FT02-B03 ('Could you build a VM?'), what is the power move after the ordered steps?
choices: 'I can whiteboard the whole flow right now if you'd like' — convert verbal to demonstration
quiz.explain: The whiteboard offer converts a question into a demo. Interviewers remember it.

quiz.q: A 'likely' probe stumps you. What is the scored response?
choices: 'I haven't hit that in production yet. Here's how I'd figure it out: [method].' — honesty + method
quiz.explain: Honesty + method beats bluffing; bluffing is detectable and fatal at a security company.

quiz.q: How do you convert a generic patching answer into a 3/3?
choices: Anchor it: 'I learned the discipline maintaining my homelab hosts — patch one node, validate, roll, snapshot before each ring'
quiz.explain: Real + short beats generic + long. Your evidence inventory is the anchor bank.

quiz.q: What is the Day 3 drill for this bank?
choices: Random sampling: 15 questions across categories, no warm-up, no cherry-picking, aloud and recorded
quiz.explain: Random sampling under mild pressure is what converts study into performance.

modules.summary: Sixty interview questions across eight categories. Nine are publicly reported by ThreatLocker candidates on Glassdoor (marked 'reported by candidates' with context); the rest are likely probes authored for this infrastructure role (marked 'likely'). Model answers are starting points — rebuild each in your own words and anchor it to something you have actually done.

cards.back: Situation (context) → Task (your responsibility) → Action (what YOU did, specifically) → Result (outcome + lesson). Under two minutes. End on the lesson.

cards.front: The honesty tripwires — what never to say
cards.back: Never 'completed' the bootcamp (enrolled Sept 30). Never invent employers, metrics, or team sizes. Never claim certifications you don't hold. If pressed, say 'I don't have that yet — here's what I do have.'
Work ethic, preparation, handling pressure. 'I treated preparation like an engineering problem with a deadline.'
Ownership, breadth, self-direction. 'No escalation path — every decision terminates with you.'
Technical depth, change discipline. 'Infrastructure work is change-management work.'
Quality bar, delivery, operational discipline. 'Verify before you ship.'
Ambition, honesty. 'Sell the slope, not the intercept.'
Initiative, continuous learning, why-ThreatLocker. 'Enrolled Sept 30, never completed.'
Read each Result; if you can't state what it proves about you in one sentence, sharpen the lesson.
0:00–0:20 Situation · 0:20–0:35 Task · 0:35–1:35 Action · 1:35–2:00 Result + lesson. Slow down for the lesson.
'I'd bring that same discipline here.' Use on your two strongest stories only.
Templates rehearse mechanics; real stories carry facts. Never present template content as experience.

cards.front: An interviewer asks about the bootcamp. Which answer holds the honesty line?
cards.back: 'I enrolled September 30th and have been working through the Zero Trust material since — here's what I took from the default-deny model...' — Enrolled + substance beats false completion every time — and they can verify.

cards.front: Your Action section is 20 seconds and your Situation is 90 seconds. What's wrong?
cards.back: Inverted: Action should be ~60% of the story (the scored part); Situation needs 1–2 sentences — Action is what's scored. Situation is scene-setting, not the story.

cards.front: An interviewer asks about a certification you don't hold. What is the scored response?
cards.back: 'Not yet — here's what I do have, and my plan to earn it. Want me to demonstrate the concepts?' — Honest + pivot to demonstrated competence. Evasion and invention both fail.

cards.front: What is the 'forward link' and when do you use it?
cards.back: 'I'd bring that same discipline here' — converts a past story into a future promise; use on your two strongest stories only — Scarcity keeps it meaningful. Two stories max.

items.prompt: S1 bootcamp enrollment. ≤2 min, end on the lesson.
items.answer: Situation → Task → Action → Result + lesson: 'enrolled Sept 30 to prove I understood the model, not the buzzword.'

Junior on paper → months of verifiable prep → sell trajectory: 'evaluate me on slope, not intercept.'
Blank on skills narrative → full prep marathon in one night → lesson: prepare obsessively and systematically.
S1 — conviction with a dated action.

items.prompt: 'Tell me about a time you failed.' → story?
items.answer: S4 — skipped verification once, now it's a non-negotiable gate.

items.prompt: 'Why should we hire you over experience?' → story?
items.answer: S6 + S2 — trajectory + preparation as evidence.
S5 — quality gates as ownership of others' pain; or honest 'here's my method' if no direct story.

items.prompt: Deliver the template on-call story. ≤2 min.
items.answer: 2 AM disk alert → remote in → log growth identified → archive + monitor added → lesson: the monitor made it a real resolution.

items.prompt: Rewrite the template's Result lesson in your own words.
items.answer: Any honest rephrasing that keeps outcome + transferable lesson.
