handsOnLab.deliverable: Inventory worksheet + 6 recorded real stories (2 passes) + question→story map with no gaps.
handsOnLab.checkpoint: All six stories ≤2 min, each ends on a lesson; every reported question maps to a story; templates clearly labeled.

modules.honestyNote: Every story below is grounded in his real, documented history. 'Enrolled Sept 30' — never 'completed'. 'Founder' — never an invented employer. Homelab scale stated as homelab. If a story needs a number you don't have, drop the number.

notes.title: STAR mechanics: the 15-second version, expanded
notes.body:
Situation → Task → Action → Result. Under two minutes. End on the lesson. That's the whole method — but each letter has a discipline:

- **Situation (20s):** One or two sentences of context. Not your life story — just enough that the action makes sense. Cut everything the interviewer doesn't need to evaluate you.
- **Task (15s):** What was *your* responsibility? Not the team's — yours. "I was responsible for..." is the sentence.
- **Action (60s):** What YOU did, specifically, in order. Verbs, not adjectives. This is 60% of the story — most candidates rush it and it's the part being scored.
- **Result (25s):** The outcome *plus the lesson or transferable skill*. "We migrated cleanly" is an outcome. "…and it's why I verify backups as a non-negotiable gate in every plan I write" is the lesson — and the lesson is what interviewers remember.

Worked micro-example (30 seconds total): "Situation: my homelab outgrew its storage layout. Task: migrate live data to a new RAID 0 array with zero loss. Action: I verified backups first, built the array, migrated in staged batches with checksum verification, and validated every service after cutover. Result: clean migration, zero data loss — and a reusable runbook. The lesson: infrastructure work is really change-management work; the plan matters more than the commands."

Record each story, listen back, cut filler. Two minutes max per story.

notes.title: The honesty tripwires — what never to say
notes.body:
Six STAR stories are already built in this module from your real, documented history (see the stories array). The honesty line for each:

- **Bootcamp:** "enrolled September 30th and working through it" — never "completed." They can verify; a security company *will* notice.
- **Founder:** your title is Founder and DevSecOps/Full Stack Developer at Interstitium Labs. The work was real. Don't inflate team size, revenue, or headcount.
- **Homelab:** state homelab scale plainly — "in my homelab" is a strength here, not a weakness. Interviewers respect honest homelab depth; they punish homelab-described-as-enterprise.
- **Numbers:** if a story needs a number you don't have, drop the number. A story without metrics beats a story with invented ones.
- **Certifications:** never claim one you don't hold. If pressed: "I don't have that yet — here's what I do have, and here's my plan to earn it."

Worked example — the pressed follow-up. Interviewer: "So you're Security+ certified?" Wrong: "Basically, I've studied the material." (Sounds evasive.) Right: "Not yet — I'm studying the Security+ domains now and it's in my 30/60/90 plan. What I can do today is walk you through the concepts — want me to explain how I'd apply least privilege to your endpoint fleet?" Honest, then pivot to demonstrated competence.

notes.title: Story inventory: mining your real history
notes.body:
Before mock day, run a full inventory pass so no experience goes unused. The worksheet method:

1. **Timeline sweep:** list every infrastructure thing you've built, broken, fixed, or migrated — homelab, founder work, bootcamp, the Oct 7 prep marathon. Aim for 15+ raw items; quantity first.
2. **Theme mapping:** the interview themes are ownership, troubleshooting depth, learning speed, honesty under pressure, customer empathy, and initiative. Tag each raw item with every theme it could serve.
3. **STAR-draft the top 8:** write Situation/Task/Action/Result for the eight best-tagged items. The six stories in this module are your core six; the extra two are spares for unexpected questions.
4. **The 'so what' test:** read each Result and ask "what does this prove about me as an infrastructure hire?" If you can't answer in one sentence, the story needs a sharper lesson.

Worked mini-inventory (yours, already done — verify it): bootcamp enrollment → initiative/learning speed; prep marathon → work ethic/pressure; founder work → ownership/breadth; homelab migration → technical depth/change discipline; platform shipping → quality bar/delivery; honest junior → ambition/honesty. Six stories, six themes, zero invention.

Do this pass on paper tonight. The physical act of writing surfaces stories that typing misses.

notes.title: TEMPLATE — practice only: building a STAR story from a junior scenario
notes.body:
**This is a TEMPLATE for practice, not your history.** Use it to rehearse the STAR *mechanics* on a scenario that isn't yours, so your real stories stay clean. Never present template content as your experience.

Template scenario: "A junior tech's first on-call weekend."
- **Situation:** "A monitoring alert fired at 2 AM on my first on-call weekend — a file server's disk was at 95%."
- **Task:** "I was the responder. Keep the server up until morning without data loss."
- **Action:** "I remoted in, confirmed it was log growth not user data, compressed and archived the oldest logs to secondary storage, verified the service was healthy, and wrote a disk-space monitor check so it wouldn't page blindly again."
- **Result:** "Server stayed up, no data lost. Lesson: the fix is half the job — the monitor I added afterward is what made it a real resolution."

Now the exercise: take this template and (1) time yourself delivering it in under two minutes, (2) identify which interview theme it serves (ownership + troubleshooting), (3) rewrite the Result's lesson in your own words. Then do the same with your real stories — the mechanics transfer, the content stays honest.

Why practice on templates: it separates *storytelling skill* from *your facts*. In the interview, the skill carries your facts.

notes.title: The 2-minute delivery: pacing and the lesson close
notes.body:
Two minutes is ~260 words aloud. The pacing that lands:

- **0:00–0:20 — Situation.** Slow, scene-setting. One breath per sentence.
- **0:20–0:35 — Task.** The pivot sentence: "My responsibility was..." Slightly faster — this is the bridge.
- **0:35–1:35 — Action.** Your natural pace. Ordered steps, specific verbs. This is where you earn the score — don't rush it.
- **1:35–2:00 — Result + lesson.** Slow down for the lesson. Make eye contact (or pause on the phone). The lesson is the last thing they hear — it's what they write down.

Worked example — the lesson close, three versions of the same story ending:
- Weak: "...so yeah, it worked out." (No lesson. Forgettable.)
- Okay: "...and we had zero data loss." (Outcome, no transfer.)
- Strong: "...zero data loss — and it's why verification is a non-negotiable gate in every plan I write now. I'd bring that same discipline here." (Outcome + lesson + forward link to the role.)

The forward link ("I'd bring that here") is the closer's move: it converts a past story into a future promise. Use it on your two strongest stories, not all six — scarcity keeps it meaningful.

Delivery drill: record all six stories back-to-back. Listen for filler ("um," "like," "you know"), hedging ("I kind of..."), and rushed actions. Cut, re-record. Two passes minimum before mock day.

notes.title: Mapping stories to questions — worked example
notes.body:
In the interview you don't get to choose the question — but you do choose which story answers it. Build the mapping now so retrieval is instant.

Worked mapping (yours):
| Question | Story | Why it fits |
|---|---|---|
| Why ThreatLocker? | S1 bootcamp enrollment | Proves conviction with a dated action |
| Hardest homelab problem? | S4 homelab migration | Technical depth + change discipline |
| Tell me about yourself? | S3 founder + S6 honest junior | Breadth, then trajectory framing |
| Failed? | S4 migration (verification lesson) | Failure → system → prevention |
| Frustrated customer? | S5 platform shipping (quality gates) | Ownership of other people's pain |
| Why hire you over experience? | S6 honest junior + S2 prep marathon | Trajectory + preparation as evidence |
| Coworker conflict? | S3 founder (disagree-and-commit) | Honest about background, principled |

The exercise: for each of the 9 reported questions in FT02, write the story ID you'd reach for. If any question has no story, that's a gap — draft a seventh story from your inventory (note 3) or prepare an honest "here's how I'd handle it" answer. No question should catch you without a mapped response.

The meta-skill: interviewers often ask the *same* competency three ways. When you hear the third variant, don't invent a new story — tell the best-fitting one again from a different angle. Consistency reads as depth.

objectives: Tell six STAR stories from your actual history, each under two minutes.
Map every story to the interview themes it serves.
Hold the honesty line: enrolled (not completed), founder (not employee), homelab (not enterprise) — framed as strengths.

quiz.q: An interviewer asks about the bootcamp. Which answer holds the honesty line?
choices: 'I enrolled September 30th and have been working through the Zero Trust material since — here's what I took from the default-deny model...'
quiz.explain: Enrolled + substance beats false completion every time — and they can verify.

quiz.q: Your Action section is 20 seconds and your Situation is 90 seconds. What's wrong?
choices: Inverted: Action should be ~60% of the story (the scored part); Situation needs 1–2 sentences
quiz.explain: Action is what's scored. Situation is scene-setting, not the story.

quiz.q: An interviewer asks about a certification you don't hold. What is the scored response?
choices: 'Not yet — here's what I do have, and my plan to earn it. Want me to demonstrate the concepts?'
quiz.explain: Honest + pivot to demonstrated competence. Evasion and invention both fail.

quiz.q: What is the 'forward link' and when do you use it?
choices: 'I'd bring that same discipline here' — converts a past story into a future promise; use on your two strongest stories only
quiz.explain: Scarcity keeps it meaningful. Two stories max.

quiz.q: You hear the third variant of the same competency question. What do you do?
choices: Tell the best-fitting story again from a different angle — consistency reads as depth
quiz.explain: Re-angled consistency beats invented variety.

quiz.q: What is the 'so what' test?
choices: Read each Result; if you can't state what it proves about you as a hire in one sentence, sharpen the lesson
quiz.explain: The lesson is what's remembered — test every story for it.

quiz.q: Why practice STAR mechanics on a TEMPLATE scenario?
choices: To have more stories to tell
Separates storytelling skill from your facts — the skill transfers, your real stories stay clean and honest
quiz.explain: Mechanics on templates, facts from real history. Never present template content as experience.

quiz.q: Your story runs 3 minutes. What do you cut first?
choices: Situation detail and filler — keep Action intact; the lesson close is the last thing cut
quiz.explain: Cut context and filler first. Action and lesson are the load-bearing parts.

quiz.q: Which bootcamp phrasing holds the honesty line?
choices: 'I enrolled September 30th and have been working through the Zero Trust material since'
quiz.explain: Enrolled + substance. They can verify; a security company will notice.

stories.title: The bootcamp enrollment
stories.basedOn: Enrolled in ThreatLocker's Zero Trust Cybersecurity Bootcamp on September 30, 2026 (documented).
stories.situation: I decided to pursue infrastructure work inside the cybersecurity industry and needed to prove — to myself first — that I understood the Zero Trust model, not just the buzzword.
stories.task: Build genuine working knowledge of default-deny, allowlisting, and ringfencing on a tight timeline before interviewing.

stories.title: The all-night prep marathon
stories.basedOn: October 7, 2026: overnight interview-prep session (skills rebuild, practice test, mock interview, cheat sheet) ahead of a morning interview.
stories.situation: The night before a major interview, I realized my skills narrative wasn't sharp enough — I was drawing a blank on articulating what I know.
stories.task: Rebuild my skills story, test my knowledge, and walk in prepared — in one night.
stories.action: I ran a full prep marathon: rebuilt my skills inventory, took a scored practice test, did a mock interview, and made a drive-over cheat sheet. I treated preparation like an engineering problem with a deadline.
stories.result: I walked in composed and ready. That night proved something about how I work: when something matters, I prepare obsessively and systematically, not anxiously.
stories.honestyNote: Factual: the prep session happened. Frame as discipline, not desperation.

stories.title: Founder and DevSecOps builder
stories.basedOn: Founder and DevSecOps/Full Stack Developer at Interstitium Labs (his stated title and role).
stories.situation: As a founder, there is no escalation path — every infrastructure decision, outage, and security call terminates with you.
stories.task: Design, build, secure, and operate production systems end-to-end with no team to hide behind.
stories.action: I built and operated the full stack: infrastructure, CI/CD pipelines, security controls, and production operations — learning each layer by owning its failures, not by reading about them.
stories.result: I developed the exact muscle this role needs: end-to-end ownership, systematic troubleshooting, and the habit of documenting everything because future-me is the on-call engineer.
stories.honestyNote: Founder is the title; the work was real. Don't inflate team size or revenue.

stories.title: The homelab migration
stories.basedOn: Homelab infrastructure work: RAID 0 (E:) data migration, Proton pipeline operations, Hyper-V/VM builds (documented across his projects).
stories.situation: My homelab outgrew its storage layout and I needed to migrate live data to a new RAID 0 array without losing anything.
stories.task: Plan and execute a storage migration with zero data loss and minimal service interruption.
stories.action: I verified backups first, built the array, migrated in staged batches with checksum verification, and validated every service after cutover — treating it with production change discipline.
stories.result: Clean migration, zero data loss, and a reusable runbook. It's also why I can whiteboard a VM build or a migration plan on demand — I've done the reps.
stories.honestyNote: Homelab scale, stated plainly — interviewers respect honest homelab depth.

stories.title: Shipping the knowledge platform
stories.basedOn: Built and deployed interstitiumlabs.dev / learn.interstitiumlabs.dev to production (documented).
stories.situation: I set out to build a production-grade knowledge platform — not a demo, a real deployed system.
stories.task: Ship enterprise-grade quality: no broken links, no half-finished pages, verified before every deploy.
stories.action: I built automated verification gates — link integrity, content validity, production readiness — into the deploy process, so nothing ships broken. Every deploy is verified, not hoped.
stories.result: A live production platform maintained to that bar continuously. That 'verify before you ship' discipline is exactly how I'd treat infrastructure changes here.
stories.honestyNote: Real shipped product. The quality-gate habit is the transferable point.

stories.title: The honest junior
stories.basedOn: His stated positioning: junior candidate aiming to earn senior-level capability; ThreatLocker's reported openness to cybersecurity career-starters.
stories.situation: I'm interviewing as a junior infrastructure candidate against people with more years on paper.
stories.task: Make the honest case for trajectory over tenure.
stories.action: I've spent months in focused, verifiable preparation — bootcamp enrollment, certification-track study across A+, Network+, Security+, and Windows Server, and hands-on homelab reps. I learn systems end-to-end and document everything.
stories.result: I'm not asking anyone to pretend I'm senior. I'm asking to be evaluated on trajectory, preparation, and how fast I close gaps — and this interview itself is the evidence.
stories.honestyNote: Never apologize for being junior; sell the slope, not the intercept.

modules.summary: Six STAR stories built only from verified real history: founder/DevSecOps work, homelab builds, ThreatLocker bootcamp enrollment (Sept 30, 2026), and the October 7 interview-prep marathon. No invented jobs, no invented metrics — the truth, structured to land.

modules.formatFraming: ThreatLocker publicly described a three-step process for its Senior Technical Support Specialist role: (1) technical phone interview, (2) product demo presentation back to the team, (3) onsite hands-on troubleshooting session. This mock mirrors that structure with a behavioral round added. The IT Infrastructure Specialist loop may differ.

handsOnLab.title: Full mock day — four rounds, scored
handsOnLab.brief: Run all four rounds back-to-back with 5-minute breaks, score each immediately, and execute the same-day re-take loop on every sub-pass round.
steps: Set up: quiet room, phone recording, printed scorecards, FT02 bank + 3 R3 scenarios + R2 talk outline.
Round 1 (20 min): 8 sampled FT02 questions, 90s each, aloud. Score immediately.
5-min break. Round 2 (30 min): 10-min hardening talk + 20 min FT02 follow-ups. Score.
5-min break. Round 3 (30 min): 3 scenarios × 10 min, thinking aloud. Score.
5-min break. Round 4 (15 min): 3 STAR stories + why ThreatLocker + why hire you. Score.
Tally: every round at/above pass mark? For any round below: 30-min targeted study, re-take weak questions same day.

notes.title: How the mock works: rules, scoring, re-take protocol
notes.body:
Four timed, scored rounds modeled on the interview structure ThreatLocker publicly described for an IT-adjacent role (technical phone screen → demo presentation → onsite troubleshooting), plus a behavioral round. Honest framing: the Infrastructure Specialist loop may differ — you prepare for all formats.

The rules:
- **Rounds 1–4 back-to-back** on mock day, in order, with only 5-minute breaks. This simulates interview fatigue — round 4 is where unprepared candidates collapse.
- **Aloud, always.** Silent "thinking" doesn't count. Record every round (phone voice memo is fine).
- **Score immediately after each round** using the rubrics below. No generosity: a 2 is "correct," a 3 is "correct + evidence." Most first attempts land 1s and 2s — that's the point.
- **Overall pass: all four rounds at or above their pass marks.** Any round below → targeted study of its weakest questions → re-take the same day. The re-take is non-negotiable; walking away from a failed round teaches your brain that failing is acceptable.
- **Question sources:** Round 1 samples 8 from the FT02 bank (mix reported + likely). Round 2 is the whiteboard talk. Round 3 uses the three scenarios below. Round 4 uses FT02 behavioral + your six STAR stories.

What you're really training: starting answers under pressure, thinking aloud, recovering from blanks, and finishing strong when tired. The content is FT02/FT03 — the mock is the *performance* layer on top.

notes.title: Round 1: phone screen tactics — worked example
notes.body:
20 minutes, 8 questions, 90 seconds each. On a phone screen there is no whiteboard and no body language — your voice is the entire signal. Tactics:

- **Number your structure aloud:** "Three things I'd check: first..." Numbering keeps you from rambling and signals organized thinking through audio alone.
- **Verdict first:** give the conclusion in the first 10 seconds, then the method. On the phone, interviewers decide early; don't bury the lead.
- **Name the nouns:** gpresult, repadmin, VHDX, Get-ADUser — specific tool names are credibility through a phone line.
- **End with an offer:** "I can go deeper on any of those" — invites the follow-up you want.

Worked example — the round 1 answer that scores 3/3. Question: "A GPO isn't applying to a user."
> "Verdict: it's a scope issue until proven otherwise. Three things I'd check, in order: first, gpresult /r on the affected machine to see what's applied and what's denied — that tells me whether it's scope or something stranger. Second, the link itself: is the user in the linked OU, link order, Enforced versus Block Inheritance, security filtering, WMI filters. Third, replication — is the DC I'm checking actually converged? Then gpupdate /force and re-check. I've hit exactly this in my homelab with a workstation baseline policy — turned out to be security filtering I'd set and forgotten. The method is: verify with gpresult, fix the scope, don't re-link randomly."

Score it: verdict (✓), ordered method with named tools (✓), real evidence (✓), 90 seconds (✓) → 3/3. Now sample 8 from FT02 and do the same for each.

notes.title: Round 2: the 10-minute demo talk — full outline, worked example
notes.body:
ThreatLocker publicly described a demo-presentation step for an IT-adjacent role: present back to the team. Your topic: "How I would harden and document a new Windows Server for a Zero Trust environment." Ten minutes, whiteboard or screen share, then 20 minutes of follow-up questions from FT02.

The outline (memorize the skeleton, not the script):
1. **Problem frame (1 min):** "A new server is an untrusted asset until proven otherwise. My job: make it known-good, least-privilege, and auditable before it touches production."
2. **Approach (2 min):** Baseline-first: patched gold image or clean install + updates; remove unneeded roles/features; local admin hygiene (LAPS-style thinking, no shared passwords).
3. **Demo (4 min):** Walk the controls: firewall profile, Defender posture, BitLocker where applicable, service minimization, audit policy, documentation of every change. *Draw* the server with its trust boundaries as you talk.
4. **Trade-offs (2 min):** "Hardening is never free — every disabled service is a potential break. My rule: disable with documentation and a rollback note, so the next admin knows why."
5. **Questions (1 min + 20 min follow-up):** "What would you challenge in this approach?" — inviting critique shows confidence.

Worked opening (the first 60 seconds, verbatim-ish — then make it yours):
> "If I unbox a Windows Server today, I treat it as hostile until I've made it otherwise. My hardening sequence is: one, get it to a known-good state — fully patched, nothing extra installed. Two, shrink the attack surface — remove unneeded roles and features, disable unneeded services, and set the firewall to deny-by-default with explicit allows. Three, identity hygiene — no shared local admin passwords, dedicated admin accounts, and audit policy on from the start. Four, document everything as I go, because an undocumented hardened server is a server nobody can maintain. Let me walk you through each layer..."

Scoring: clarity 0–6, technical accuracy 0–6, handling questions 0–6, time discipline 0–6. Pass ≥17/24. The trap: rambling past 10 minutes. Finish at 9, not 11.

notes.title: Round 3: thinking aloud — worked example
notes.body:
30 minutes, 3 scenarios, 10 minutes each. The meta-skill: narrate your methodology. Interviewers score the thinking they can *hear*, not the answer you reach silently.

The narration template: "I'm checking X first because [reason]. That gives me [information], which tells me whether to go to Y or Z."

Worked example — scenario (a): "A user can't reach the file share."
> "Okay — first I need to know the blast radius, so I'm asking: is it one user or everyone? One user — that rules out the server itself for now, so I'm looking at the client and the path. I'm checking the physical layer first because it's cheapest to rule out: cable, port, can they reach anything else? They can reach the intranet — so L1/L2 and their local stack are fine, and it's specific to the share. Next I'd check name resolution versus the share itself: can they ping the server by name? By IP? If IP works but the name doesn't, it's DNS. If both work but the share fails, I'm looking at SMB and permissions — and I'd check whether their password recently changed, because cached credentials cause exactly this. At each step I'm ruling out a layer before moving deeper, so I don't chase three hypotheses at once."

What the interviewer heard: blast-radius discipline, layered method, cheapest-test-first, a specific gotcha (cached credentials), and hypothesis control. That's 4/4 on methodology even before the diagnosis lands.

Scenario (b) GPO: narrate the gpresult-first method from FT02-W02. Scenario (c) VM lost network: narrate the virtual-switch check (external/internal/private), then the guest's network config — "the most common cause after a change is the change itself, so I'm looking at what moved." Always narrate *why this check before that one*.

notes.title: Round 4: behavioral delivery — worked example
notes.body:
15 minutes, 5 answers: 3 STAR stories + "why ThreatLocker" + "why hire you." By round 4 you're tired — that's the test. Tactics:

- **Lead with your strongest story.** Don't save it. A strong first answer sets the interviewer's pen moving in the right direction.
- **The stories are already built (FT03).** Round 4 is delivery, not invention. If you catch yourself inventing, stop — tell a real one again from a different angle.
- **"Why ThreatLocker" and "why hire you" are closers.** End each with the forward link: "...which is why I'm here" / "...evaluate me on trajectory."

Worked example — "Why should we hire you over a more experienced candidate?" (the hardest 60 seconds of the day):
> "I won't pretend to have years I don't have — so here's the honest case. What I offer is trajectory: I learn systems end-to-end instead of memorizing steps, I document everything, and I prepare obsessively — this interview is the evidence. I enrolled in your Zero Trust bootcamp on September 30th, I've spent six days in structured prep, and I can whiteboard a VM build, narrate a file-share triage, and defend the default-deny model right now, cold. You'd be hiring someone with no bad habits to unlearn and a demonstrated slope. I'm asking to be evaluated on that."

Score it: honesty without apology (✓), specific dated evidence (✓), demonstration offer (✓), forward framing (✓) → 3/3. Then stop. The biggest round-4 failure is the ramble-after-the-answer — when you're done, you're done.

notes.title: Scoring yourself honestly + the re-take loop — worked example scorecard
notes.body:
Score immediately after each round. The rubric, per question: 0 wrong/silent, 1 vague, 2 correct, 3 correct + evidence. Round pass marks: R1 ≥17/24, R2 ≥17/24, R3 ≥25/36, R4 ≥11/15.

Worked example — a filled R1 scorecard:
| # | Question | Score | Note |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Build a VM? | 3 | Steps + whiteboard offer, 85s |
| 2 | GPO not applying? | 2 | Method right, no evidence anchor |
| 3 | TCP vs UDP? | 2 | Correct, rushed the examples |
| 4 | Checkpoint vs backup? | 3 | "Checkpoint is NOT a backup" landed |
| 5 | Zero Trust plain language? | 1 | Rambled, no skeleton, 2 min+ |
| 6 | EDR flag? | 2 | Missed "preserve evidence" |
| 7 | Subnetting for a manager? | 1 | Jargon dump, no analogy |
| 8 | Why ThreatLocker? | 3 | Conviction + bootcamp date |
| Total | | 17/24 | PASS — but 5 and 7 are re-take targets |

The re-take loop (same day, non-negotiable):
1. **Isolate:** only the sub-pass questions (here: #5, #7, plus #2's missing anchor, #6's missed step).
2. **Targeted study:** 30 minutes on exactly those — rewrite using verdict → method → evidence → close.
3. **Re-take:** re-answer just those four, aloud, timed. All must hit 2+.
4. **Log it:** write the date, the round, the weak questions, and what fixed them. This log is your trajectory evidence — and it kills the anxiety of "am I actually improving?" because the numbers say so.

Rule: a failed round re-taken the same day counts double in your confidence. A failed round postponed counts zero.

modules.overallRule: Overall pass: all four rounds at or above their pass marks. Any round below → targeted study of its weakest questions → re-take the same day.

quiz.q: In Round 1 (phone screen), why do you number your structure aloud?
choices: No whiteboard or body language — numbering keeps you from rambling and signals organized thinking through audio alone
quiz.explain: Voice is the entire signal on a phone screen; structure must be audible.

quiz.q: Your Round 2 talk runs 13 minutes. What is the scoring consequence?
choices: Time discipline is 6 of 24 points; finishing at 9 beats rambling to 13. Cut to fit.
quiz.explain: Time discipline is scored. Finish early rather than ramble.

quiz.q: In Round 3, you reach the right diagnosis silently, then announce it. What did you lose?
choices: Methodology points: interviewers score the thinking they can hear. Narrate why this check before that one.
quiz.explain: The meta-skill is audible methodology, not silent correctness.

quiz.q: Round 4, you're tired and inventing details in a story. What is the correct recovery?
choices: Stop. Tell a real story again from a different angle. Invention is detectable and fatal.
quiz.explain: Delivery, not invention. Consistency reads as depth.

quiz.q: Your R1 scorecard totals 15/24. What happens next?
choices: Same-day re-take loop: isolate weak questions → 30 min targeted study → re-answer aloud → log the fix
quiz.explain: Below pass mark → targeted re-take the same day. Non-negotiable.

quiz.q: What is the single highest-leverage line in the VM-build answer?
choices: 'I can whiteboard the whole flow right now if you'd like' — converts verbal to demonstration
quiz.explain: The whiteboard offer is the power move interviewers remember.

quiz.q: Why do rounds run back-to-back with only 5-minute breaks?
choices: Simulates interview fatigue — round 4 is where unprepared candidates collapse. Train tired.
quiz.explain: Performance under fatigue is a separate skill. Train it deliberately.

quiz.q: A follow-up question exposes a gap in your Round 2 talk. What scores best?
choices: 'Good challenge — here's how I'd think about it...' then reason aloud from the model. Honesty + method.
quiz.explain: Handling questions is 6 of 24 points in R2. Reason aloud; never bluff.

quiz.q: What does the re-take log give you beyond the scores?
choices: Trajectory evidence — dated proof you're improving, which kills 'am I actually getting better?' anxiety
quiz.explain: The log turns feelings into numbers. Numbers compound confidence.

notes.title: Why logistics win interviews before they start
notes.body:
Interviews are scored from the first handshake. A candidate who arrives flustered, late, or digging through a bag for a resume starts at a deficit no technical answer fully erases. Logistics are the only part of the interview you control completely — so control them completely.

The psychology, briefly: interviewers are pattern-matching for "can I trust this person with my infrastructure?" Punctuality, preparation, and composure are *evidence* of operational discipline — the same discipline that prevents outages. When you arrive 20 minutes early with printed resumes and a calm demeanor, you've already answered "are you reliable?" before the first question.

The corollary: no amount of logistics saves bad answers. FT05 doesn't replace FT01–FT04 — it protects the investment you made in them. Think of it as the change-management wrapper around the technical deployment: the deployment (your knowledge) only lands if the change window (the day) is executed cleanly.

notes.title: Day-before walkthrough with rationale
notes.body:
Each day-before item exists for a reason. Walk it with the reasoning attached:

1. **Confirm the address from the invitation email.** See the location note below — there are two candidate addresses. The invitation is the authority. Map the route; drive it if possible. (Rationale: navigation failure is the #1 preventable cause of lateness.)
2. **Print 5 copies of your resume on clean paper + one-page portfolio summary** (homelab builds, bootcamp enrollment Sept 30, cert track). (Rationale: interviewers share resumes; handing a crisp copy to each person signals preparation. The portfolio summary is your evidence sheet — it does the bragging so you don't have to.)
3. **Lay out professional attire; pack the bag** (resumes, portfolio summary, notebook + pen, photo ID, references list, phone charger, water). (Rationale: every item packed tonight is one decision you don't make under morning adrenaline.)
4. **Light review only: the 9 reported questions + 6 STAR stories, once. No cramming after 8 PM.** (Rationale: cramming the night before degrades sleep, and sleep is performance. You prepared for six days; trust the work.)
5. **Two alarms. Sleep by 10:30 PM.** (Rationale: a single alarm is a single point of failure. You of all people should know better — no SPOFs.)

The theme: eliminate morning decisions, eliminate single points of failure, protect sleep. You're applying infrastructure discipline to yourself.

Worked example — the 07:00 review, exactly: stand up, phone timer, deliver "why ThreatLocker" (45s), the VM-build walkthrough (90s), S4 homelab migration (2 min). Total under 5 minutes. Then close the materials. If your brain screams "one more topic!" — that's anxiety, not a gap. The six days were the preparation; the morning is the performance.

notes.title: Location verification protocol
notes.body:
Plan anchor: **1950 W Maitland Blvd, Orlando** — per the interview invitation details provided. This is the address you navigate to.

The conflict you must resolve: ThreatLocker's public listings show its headquarters at **1950 Summit Park Drive, Orlando, FL 32810**. Two addresses, one company. The protocol:

1. **The invitation email is the authority.** Re-read it the night before. If it says Maitland Blvd, you go to Maitland Blvd.
2. **If the invitation is ambiguous**, check the Calendly confirmation (booked via Crawford Thomas / Alex Starr) — it should restate the location.
3. **If still ambiguous**, email Alex Starr the day before: "Confirming tomorrow's 9:00 AM interview location — 1950 W Maitland Blvd?" One short email beats driving to the wrong building.
4. **Have both addresses in your maps app.** If you arrive and the building looks wrong, you have the fallback ready without panic.

Worked example — the drive-by: the night before, you map 1950 W Maitland Blvd, note the parking situation on satellite view, and save 1950 Summit Park Drive as a second pin labeled "HQ fallback." Morning-of, you drive to the invitation address. Total extra effort: 4 minutes. Total risk removed: arriving at the wrong building for a 9:00 AM interview.

Never assume. Verify. This is the same discipline as verifying backups before a migration — the stakes are just more visible.

notes.title: The 5-minute reset + the 'I don't know' protocol
notes.body:
Two micro-skills for the waiting room and the hot seat.

**The 5-minute reset** (in your car or the lobby, before you're called):
1. Arrive → 2. Breathe: 4 counts in, 6 out, 3 rounds → 3. Recall one STAR story (your strongest — S4 or S1) → 4. Say to yourself: "trajectory, preparation, honesty" → 5. Walk in.

The breathing isn't mysticism — it down-regulates the adrenaline spike so your prefrontal cortex (the part that answers technical questions) stays online. The story recall puts you in "I have evidence" mode instead of "I hope they go easy" mode. The three words are your identity anchor for the day.

**The 'I don't know' protocol** — because you *will* get a question you can't answer, and how you handle it is scored:
> "I haven't hit that in production yet. Here's how I'd figure it out: [method]."

Worked example. Question: "How would you configure ThreatLocker's Network Control for a multi-site deployment?" (You don't know their console.) Weak: bluffing about console screens you've never seen — fatal at a security company. Strong: "I haven't worked in the console itself — my knowledge is from your public platform materials. Here's how I'd approach it from first principles: I'd start by mapping what each site's endpoints need to reach, default-deny everything else, and build the policy in monitor mode before enforcing, so I can see what would break before it breaks. And I'd lean on your team's console expertise for the click-path — I'm here to learn the tool, I already understand the model."

Honesty + method + forward lean. That's a 2/3 on a question you couldn't answer — which beats the 0/3 (plus trust damage) of a bluff, every time.

notes.title: After: the thank-you note — worked example
notes.body:
Send within 2 hours of leaving. Email to the interviewer(s) — via Alex Starr at Crawford Thomas if you don't have direct addresses. Three sentences, one specific reference.

Worked example:
> Subject: Thank you — IT Infrastructure Specialist interview
>
> [Name], thank you for the conversation this morning. I particularly enjoyed the discussion about [something specific — e.g., "how your team thinks about default-deny in practice" or "the troubleshooting scenario you walked me through"] — it confirmed what drew me to ThreatLocker in the first place.
>
> I'm excited about the possibility of contributing to the team. Please let me know if there's anything else I can provide.
>
> Best, Enmanuel Mejia · (617) 299-0781 · mejiaenmanueld@gmail.com

Why it works: the specific reference proves you were present and listening (most thank-yous are generic). The contact block makes follow-up frictionless. What it doesn't do: beg, grovel, or re-litigate answers you wish you'd nailed — never "by the way, what I meant to say about subnets was..."

Then: log the interview while it's fresh — who you met, what they asked, what you'd improve. That log is gold whether there's a second round or a next opportunity.

notes.title: The no-promise framing — read this first
notes.body:
No hiring promise is made or implied by this module, this course, or your preparation. You are preparing to *handle* an offer professionally if one comes — not expecting one. That distinction matters for two reasons:

1. **Desperation leaks.** Candidates who act like the offer is certain (or desperately needed) negotiate badly and interview anxiously. The mindset is: "I'm preparing for every outcome, including a no — and a no just means the next rep."
2. **The screening is real either way.** Public postings describe a background check and drug/substance screening after a conditional offer. Being ready for that step is professionalism, not presumption.

Worked mindset check — say these aloud and mean them:
- "My preparation earns me the best possible performance. The outcome is not mine to control."
- "If the answer is no, I keep the thank-you, the log, and the reps — and I go again."
- "If the answer is yes, I evaluate calmly, not euphorically."

This module is the 30/60/90 plan, the offer evaluation worksheet, and the screening prep. Professional handling of success is a skill — train it like the rest.

notes.title: Evaluating an offer: total compensation — worked example
notes.body:
Never accept on the spot from excitement. Take the full decision window. Evaluate *total* compensation, not just salary:

**Worked example — the evaluation worksheet (fill with real numbers when the offer comes):**
```
Base salary:            $______ /yr        (your stated target: $90,000)
Bonus / variable:       $______            (ask: is it guaranteed or target-based?)
Health insurance:       $______ /mo employee cost  (ask: what plan, what deductible?)
PTO / holidays:         ______ days        (ask: accrual vs lump, rollover?)
Retirement match:       ______ %           (ask: vesting schedule?)
Training/cert budget:   $______ /yr        (ask explicitly — funds your Security+/AZ path)
On-call expectations:   ________________   (ask: rotation, compensation, frequency)
Growth path:            ________________   (ask: what does year 2 look like?)
Start date flexibility: ________________
```

**The questions to ask (in writing, before deciding):**
- "Can you confirm the role scope — title, team, primary responsibilities, on-call expectations?"
- "What does the certification and training support look like?" (Signals growth culture AND funds your path.)
- "What is the decision timeline on your side?" (Gives you the window without seeming hesitant.)

**Red flags that warrant a pause:** pressure to decide same-day, scope that shifts between conversations, unwillingness to put the offer in writing, on-call described as "occasional" with no rotation defined. None of these are accusations — they're clarifications you request calmly, in writing.

Worked example — the stall, done gracefully: "Thank you — I'm excited about this. I want to give it the careful consideration it deserves; can I confirm by [date]?" Professional, unhurried, respectful of both sides.

notes.title: Negotiation scripts for a junior candidate — worked examples
notes.body:
Junior candidates can negotiate — the leverage is *competing optionality and demonstrated value*, not years. Three scripts:

**Script 1 — the number is below target:** "Thank you for the offer. Based on my research for infrastructure specialist roles in Orlando and the preparation I've invested in your stack specifically, I was targeting closer to $90,000. Is there flexibility to bridge that gap?" (Calm, researched, specific number. Then *stop talking* — silence is the negotiation tool.)

**Script 2 — the number is fine but growth matters:** "The base works for me. What I'd love to understand is the growth path — what does progression look like in the first 18 months, and is there training budget for the Security+ and AZ-800 I'm pursuing?" (Trades salary pressure for career capital — often easier for them to say yes to.)

**Script 3 — they say the number is firm:** "I understand. Two things would make this an easy yes: [training budget / start date / PTO day]. Are any of those flexible?" (When salary is fixed, negotiate the package around it.)

**Rules:**
- Everything material in writing before you accept. Verbal promises evaporate.
- Never lie about competing offers. ("I have another offer at $X" when you don't is detectable and destroys trust.)
- Your stated desired salary ($90,000/yr, from your applications) is your anchor — don't negotiate against yourself by naming a lower number first.
- One round of negotiation is normal; three rounds is adversarial. Ask once, well.

notes.title: Screening prep: what the public postings describe
notes.body:
ThreatLocker's publicly posted roles describe a **background check and drug/substance screening after a conditional offer**. This is their standard process — expect it, don't fear it. Preparation:

1. **Keep a valid photo ID ready** — the same ID you bring to the interview.
2. **Ensure your references are warned and reachable.** Call them *before* the offer: "You may get a reference check from ThreatLocker/Crawford Thomas in the next two weeks — are you still good to speak for me?" A surprised reference is a weak reference.
3. **Keep your documented history consistent** with what you stated in interviews — dates, titles, bootcamp enrollment (Sept 30, *enrolled*). Inconsistency between interview statements and screening forms is the #1 self-inflicted wound.
4. **Disclose proactively if asked.** If a form asks about anything in your history, answer truthfully and briefly. The screening verifies; it doesn't interrogate — unless you give it a reason to.

Worked example — the reference warning call (do this now, before any offer): "Hi [Name] — quick heads-up: I'm in final stages for an IT Infrastructure Specialist role at ThreatLocker in Orlando. If they call, they'd ask about [reliability / technical ability / character]. Still comfortable speaking for me? I'll send you the role description so you're not blindsided." Two minutes, massive difference in reference quality.

Timeline note: screening happens *after* a conditional offer — it is not part of the interview day. Don't bring it up unprompted in the interview; handle it when the offer letter arrives.

notes.title: The 30/60/90 plan — worked example (his actual plan)
notes.body:
Write this on one page. Bring it if a final-round conversation invites it — unprompted is fine only if the moment fits ("What would your first 90 days look like?" is the invitation; don't force it).

**Days 1–30: LEARN**
- Document the environment as you discover it — network map, AD structure, ticket queues, escalation paths. Your documentation habit is your onboarding superpower.
- Ask questions constantly; write down every answer. Nobody expects output in week one — they expect *absorption*.
- Complete compliance, security, and tooling onboarding without being chased.
- Shadow escalations. Take notes on how seniors triage — that's your real training.

**Days 31–60: CONTRIBUTE**
- Own L2 tickets end-to-end: triage → resolve → document → close. Become the person whose tickets don't bounce back.
- Propose one documentation improvement — the gap you found while learning. (Contributing docs in month two signals ownership.)
- Start Security+ study in earnest — 30 minutes a day, non-negotiable.

**Days 61–90: LEAD (something small)**
- Own a small infrastructure improvement end-to-end — a GPO cleanup, a monitoring gap closed, a runbook written.
- Present a 15-minute lunch-and-learn on something you learned (e.g., "What I learned about our ticketing patterns in 60 days").
- Have AZ-800 booked or Security+ scheduled. Certifications in flight prove the trajectory you sold in the interview.

Worked one-line version (the card): 30: learn the environment and document it. 60: contribute independently and start certifying. 90: lead something small and teach something back.

Why this plan wins: it's *specific* (not "learn the ropes"), it's *documented* (your differentiator), and every phase has a visible artifact. Interviewers don't just hear ambition — they hear execution.

notes.title: First-week behaviors that earn trust — worked example
notes.body:
The offer is signed. Now the real interview begins — the first two weeks, when everyone forms their permanent impression. Behaviors that earn trust fast:

1. **Write everything down, then share it.** Your day-3 network map draft, posted for correction, earns more trust than a month of silent competence. Seniors *love* juniors who document — it means they don't have to.
2. **Ask the question, then the follow-up.** "How do we handle this?" then "Why is it done that way?" The second question is what separates learners from ticket-closers.
3. **Close the loop visibly.** "You asked me to check X — here's what I found, here's the doc." Reliability is demonstrated in small completions, not grand promises.
4. **Learn names and roles in week one.** The fastest way to get help in month three is to have been genuinely curious in week one.
5. **Protect the honesty line forever.** "I don't know, but here's how I'd find out" works on day 5 exactly as well as it worked in the interview. The day you bluff at work is the day the interview honesty becomes a lie.

Worked example — the first-week win: On day 4, you notice the onboarding wiki's VPN setup steps are outdated (you just lived them). You update the page, note the change in the team channel, and move on. Cost: 20 minutes. Signal sent: this person improves the environment they touch, documents without being asked, and doesn't wait for permission to fix small things. That's the entire 30/60/90 plan in miniature — and it's how "junior" becomes "trusted" faster than tenure would predict.

modules.title: Prereq Math: Discrete Mathematics for IT Infrastructure
modules.summary: Sets, counting rules, permutations and combinations, the pigeonhole principle, and graph basics — the math of CIDR blocks, password spaces, and scheduling. Prerequisite spine for IT Infrastructure.
objectives: Use set operations and inclusion–exclusion.
Count with the sum/product rules, permutations, and combinations.
Apply the pigeonhole principle.
Use the handshaking lemma on small graphs.

notes.title: Why this math matters for IT Infrastructure
notes.body:
**Relevance.** IP addressing, subnetting, and binary/hex are discrete mathematics. This module formalizes the number systems you use daily.

Work this module before the technical modules it supports: the worked examples below are fully computed (verify each with the Python lab), and the drills test the exact calculations you will reuse. Math done by hand once beats math skimmed ten times.

notes.title: Sets and inclusion–exclusion
notes.body: A set is an unordered collection of distinct elements. Union ∪, intersection ∩, complement, difference \. |A| is cardinality. Inclusion–exclusion: |A∪B| = |A|+|B|−|A∩B| — add both, subtract the double-count. Worked example (verified): 120 hosts; 45 run Linux (L), 70 run Windows (W), 25 run both (dual-boot). |L∪W| = 45+70−25 = 90. Hosts running neither: 120−90 = 30. Three-set version adds back the triple intersection: |A∪B∪C| = Σ|A|−Σ|A∩B|+|A∩B∩C|. Venn diagrams are this formula drawn. In monitoring, "alerts from source A or source B" is a union — deduplicate the overlap or you double-count incidents.

notes.title: The sum and product rules
notes.body: Sum rule: if task 1 has n ways and task 2 has m disjoint ways, the combined choice has n+m. Product rule: for sequential independent choices, n×m. Worked example (verified): passwords of length 3 over lowercase letters (26) with the first character a vowel (5). Choices: 5×26×26 = 5×676 = 3380. If instead the rule is "vowel somewhere" the counting gets harder (inclusion–exclusion territory) — a warning that constraints interact. Product rule powers CIDR math: a /24 has 2^8 = 256 addresses because each of 8 host bits is an independent binary choice. Sum rule powers case analysis: total outcomes = sum over disjoint cases.

notes.title: Permutations: order matters
notes.body: P(n,k) = n!/(n−k)! counts ordered selections of k from n. Worked example (verified): P(5,3) = 5×4×3 = 60 — ways to award gold/silver/bronze among 5 finalists. Full permutations P(n,n) = n!. Scheduling n distinct jobs on one machine: n! orders (5 jobs → 120 orders). Permutations with repetition: n^k (each of k positions has n choices) — a 4-digit PIN has 10^4 = 10000 possibilities. Distinguish "ordered" from "unordered" before reaching for a formula: medals are ordered (who gets gold matters); committees are not.

notes.title: Combinations: order doesn’t matter
notes.body: C(n,k) = n!/(k!(n−k)!) counts k-subsets of an n-set. Worked example (verified): C(10,3) = 10×9×8/(3×2×1) = 720/6 = 120 — ways to choose a 3-person review panel from 10 engineers. Symmetry: C(n,k) = C(n,n−k) (choosing who’s IN equals choosing who’s OUT): C(10,7) = 120 ✓. Pascal’s identity: C(n,k) = C(n−1,k−1)+C(n−1,k) — each subset either includes element n or not. Binomial theorem: (x+y)^n = ΣC(n,k)x^k y^(n−k); setting x=y=1 gives Σ2^n subsets total. Subnetting is combinations in disguise: choosing which host bits vary.

notes.title: The pigeonhole principle
notes.body: If n+1 items go into n boxes, some box holds ≥2 items. Generalized: n items into k boxes ⇒ some box holds ≥ ⌈n/k⌉. Worked example (verified): among 13 people, two share a birth month (13 > 12) ✓. Stronger: among 25 people, some month has ⌈25/12⌉ = ⌈2.083⌉ = 3 people ✓. Hash collisions are pigeonholes: 2^64 possible inputs into 2^32 hash slots guarantees collisions — the birthday bound says they appear after ~2^16 ≈ 77k inputs for 32-bit hashes (more precisely ~√(2^32)). Dirichlet’s principle also proves: any 6 people contain 3 mutual acquaintances or 3 mutual strangers (Ramsey R(3,3)=6) — a party trick with a real proof.

notes.title: Graphs and the handshaking lemma
notes.body: A graph has vertices V and edges E (unordered pairs). Degree deg(v) = incident edge count. Handshaking lemma: Σdeg(v) = 2|E| — every edge contributes 2 to the degree sum. Corollary: the number of odd-degree vertices is even. Worked example (verified): a network with 5 routers and 6 links. Degrees: A:3, B:2, C:3, D:2, E:2. Sum = 3+2+3+2+2 = 12 = 2×6 ✓. Odd-degree vertices: A, C (two of them — even count ✓). Eulerian trail (use every edge once) exists iff 0 or 2 vertices have odd degree — this graph qualifies (A…C trail). Network topology, dependency graphs, and state machines are graphs; the lemma is a 10-second sanity check on any degree data ("sum is odd ⇒ your data is wrong").

cards.back: |A|+|B|−|A∩B| — subtract the double-count.
60 (5×4×3) — ordered selections.
120 — 3-person panels from 10.
C(n,n−k) — symmetry.
Two share a month (13 > 12).
Σdeg(v) = 2|E|; odd-degree vertex count is even.
Sum: disjoint alternatives (n+m). Product: sequential choices (n×m).
10^4 = 10000 (repetition allowed).

0 or 2 odd-degree vertices.
2^8 = 256 — 8 independent binary host-bit choices.

handsOnLab.title: Verify counting with Python
handsOnLab.brief: You will verify permutations, combinations, inclusion–exclusion, the pigeonhole principle, and the handshaking lemma by brute-force enumeration in Python. Formulas must match exhaustive counts.
steps: Open python3. From math import comb, perm, factorial. Assert comb(10,3)==120 and perm(5,3)==60.
Brute-force C(10,3): from itertools import combinations; assert len(list(combinations(range(10),3)))==120.
Inclusion–exclusion: build sets L (45 even numbers <90), W (70 multiples of 3 <210) over a 120-element universe with 25 overlap by construction; assert |L∪W| == 45+70-25.
Pigeonhole: assign 13 random birth months (1..12) 10k times; assert every trial has a collision.
Handshaking: build the notes’ graph as an edge list with 6 edges; compute degrees; assert sum == 12 and odd-degree count is even.
Break-it: compute comb(100,50) — observe the huge integer; then time permutations of 10 vs 11 to feel factorial growth.
Write up: which enumerations matched the formulas, and the timing numbers for factorial growth.
handsOnLab.deliverable: Write-up with verification outputs and the factorial timing comparison.
handsOnLab.checkpoint: All asserts pass; brute-force counts match formulas; timing shows the factorial blowup.

mockTask.explain: Choose then order: C(10,3)×3! = 120×6 = 720 = P(10,3). Two-stage counting: combinations then permutations.

modules.title: Prereq Math: Logic & Proof for IT Infrastructure
modules.summary: Propositional logic, truth tables, quantifiers, and the four proof methods (direct, contrapositive, contradiction, induction) — the reasoning substrate for policies, algorithms, and security arguments. Prerequisite spine for IT Infrastructure.
objectives: Evaluate compound propositions with truth tables and identify tautologies.
Apply De Morgan’s laws and logical equivalences to simplify statements.
Negate quantified statements correctly (∀/∃ duality).
Write direct, contrapositive, contradiction, and induction proofs.

notes.title: Why this math matters for IT Infrastructure
notes.body:
**Relevance.** Troubleshooting is logical inference: eliminating hypotheses, reasoning from symptoms. This module sharpens the method.

Work this module before the technical modules it supports: the worked examples below are fully computed (verify each with the Python lab), and the drills test the exact calculations you will reuse. Math done by hand once beats math skimmed ten times.

notes.title: Propositions, connectives, and truth tables
notes.body: A proposition is a statement that is either true (T) or false (F) — never both. The connectives build compounds: negation ¬p, conjunction p∧q (and), disjunction p∨q (or, inclusive), implication p→q (if p then q), biconditional p↔q (p iff q). A truth table enumerates every input combination: n variables need 2^n rows. Worked example: build the table for p→q. Recall p→q is F only when p=T and q=F. Rows: (T,T)→T; (T,F)→F; (F,T)→T; (F,F)→T. So "if 2+2=5 then the moon is cheese" is TRUE as a material implication — the antecedent is false. This surprises beginners, but implication promises only that a true antecedent never yields a false consequent. In policy engines and code (if-statements), this is exactly the semantics: the rule fires only when the condition holds; a false condition makes the implication vacuously true.

notes.title: Tautologies, contradictions, and De Morgan’s laws
notes.body: A tautology is true in every row (e.g., p∨¬p); a contradiction is false in every row (p∧¬p). Two formulas are logically equivalent if their tables match column-for-column. Worked example (verified): prove De Morgan’s law ¬(p∧q) ≡ ¬p∨¬q by table. Row (T,T): LHS ¬T=F; RHS F∨F=F. Row (T,F): LHS ¬F=T; RHS F∨T=T. Row (F,T): LHS T; RHS T∨F=T. Row (F,F): LHS T; RHS T∨T=T. All four rows agree — equivalence verified. The dual law ¬(p∨q) ≡ ¬p∧¬q holds by the same check. These laws are the workhorses of simplifying firewall rules, IAM policies, and boolean search: "not (A and B)" becomes "not-A or not-B". Other key equivalences: contrapositive (p→q ≡ ¬q→¬p), and implication-as-disjunction (p→q ≡ ¬p∨q).

notes.title: Predicates and quantifiers
notes.body: A predicate P(x) becomes a proposition when x is fixed. Quantifiers bind x: ∀x P(x) ("for all x") and ∃x P(x) ("there exists x"). Worked example: let domain be integers, P(x) = "x² ≥ 0". Then ∀x P(x) is TRUE (squares are never negative). Now negate ∀x∃y (y > x) — "for every integer there is a larger one". Negation flips each quantifier and the inner predicate: ∃x∀y (y ≤ x) — "some integer is ≥ every integer", which is FALSE over integers (no maximum). The duality rules: ¬∀x P(x) ≡ ∃x ¬P(x), and ¬∃x P(x) ≡ ∀x ¬P(x). Common error: negating "all users are admins" as "no users are admins" — the correct negation is "some user is not an admin". In access-control requirements, this distinction is the difference between a correct policy and a breach.

notes.title: Direct proof and proof by contrapositive
notes.body: A direct proof assumes the hypothesis and derives the conclusion through valid steps. Proof by contrapositive proves ¬q→¬p instead of p→q (equivalent by the table). Worked example: prove "if n² is even, then n is even" for integers. Direct attack stalls (square roots of parity are awkward), so use contrapositive: "if n is odd, then n² is odd". Let n = 2k+1. Then n² = 4k²+4k+1 = 2(2k²+2k)+1, which is odd. Contrapositive proved, so the original holds. Numeric check: n=7 (odd) → 49 (odd) ✓; n=6 (even) → 36 (even) ✓. Choose the method by shape: when the conclusion is a negative or "not" statement, contrapositive usually simplifies; when hypothesis and conclusion are both positive constructions, go direct.

notes.title: Proof by contradiction
notes.body: Assume the negation of what you want, derive an impossibility, and conclude the original. Worked example (classic, verified): prove √2 is irrational. Assume √2 = a/b in lowest terms (gcd(a,b)=1). Then 2 = a²/b², so a² = 2b² — a² is even, hence a is even (by the previous note’s result), a = 2k. Then 4k² = 2b², so b² = 2k² — b² is even, hence b is even. But a and b both even contradicts lowest terms. The assumption is impossible; √2 is irrational. The pattern: contradiction proofs shine when the claim says something does NOT exist (no rational square root, no largest prime). Euclid’s proof of infinitely many primes uses the same skeleton: assume finitely many, multiply them and add 1, find a new prime factor — contradiction.

notes.title: Mathematical induction
notes.body: To prove P(n) for all n ≥ n₀: (1) base case P(n₀); (2) inductive step: assume P(k) (induction hypothesis), prove P(k+1). Worked example (verified): prove 1+2+⋯+n = n(n+1)/2. Base n=1: LHS 1, RHS 1·2/2 = 1 ✓. Assume true for k. For k+1: LHS = k(k+1)/2 + (k+1) = (k+1)(k/2+1) = (k+1)(k+2)/2 ✓ — exactly the formula at n=k+1. Numeric spot-check: n=5 gives 1+2+3+4+5=15 and 5·6/2=15 ✓; n=100 gives 5050 = 100×101/2 ✓. Induction is the proof method behind every loop-correctness argument and every recursive algorithm analysis: the base case is the loop’s first iteration, the step is "if the invariant holds entering iteration k, it holds leaving it".

cards.back: A statement that is unambiguously true or false — never both, never neither.
Only when p is true and q is false. All other rows are true (vacuous truth).
¬(p∧q) ≡ ¬p∨¬q and ¬(p∨q) ≡ ¬p∧¬q — verified by truth table.
∃x ¬P(x). Quantifier flips; inner predicate negates.

cards.front: What is the contrapositive of p→q?
cards.back: ¬q→¬p — logically equivalent to the original.

cards.front: p→q is equivalent to which disjunction?
cards.back: ¬p∨q.

cards.front: What is a tautology? A contradiction?
cards.back: Tautology: true in every truth-table row (p∨¬p). Contradiction: false in every row (p∧¬p).
Assume the negation of the claim; derive an impossibility; conclude the claim holds.

cards.front: The two steps of mathematical induction?
cards.back: Base case P(n₀); inductive step: P(k) ⇒ P(k+1).

cards.front: Prove: if n² is even then n is even. Method?
cards.back: Contrapositive: n odd ⇒ n=2k+1 ⇒ n²=2(2k²+2k)+1, odd.

quiz.q: p=F, q=T. What is p→q?
quiz.explain: Implication is false only for (T,F). With a false antecedent it is vacuously true.

quiz.q: ¬(p∨q) is equivalent to:
quiz.explain: De Morgan’s second law — verified row-by-row in the notes.

quiz.q: The contrapositive of "If the alert fires, the SOC investigates" is:
choices: If the alert does not fire, the SOC does not investigate
If the SOC does not investigate, the alert did not fire
If the SOC investigates, the alert fired
The alert fires iff the SOC investigates
quiz.explain: Contrapositive flips and negates: ¬q→¬p. (The first choice is the inverse — a different, non-equivalent statement.)

quiz.q: Negation of "Every admin has MFA enabled":
choices: Some admin does not have MFA enabled
quiz.explain: ¬∀x P(x) ≡ ∃x ¬P(x). "None do" is stronger than the negation and usually false.

quiz.q: Which is a tautology?
quiz.explain: For any p,q, at least one direction of implication holds — check all four rows. The others fail on some row.

quiz.q: To prove "there is no largest prime" you would use:
quiz.explain: Non-existence claims suit contradiction: assume finitely many primes, construct a number with a new prime factor.

quiz.q: In an induction proof of 1+⋯+n=n(n+1)/2, the inductive step shows:
quiz.explain: Assume the hypothesis at k, derive k+1: k(k+1)/2+(k+1) = (k+1)(k+2)/2.

quiz.q: p=T, q=F. Evaluate (p→q)∨(q→p).
quiz.explain: p→q is F, but q→p is T (false antecedent), and F∨T = T.

quiz.q: "If n is divisible by 4 then n is even." The converse is:
choices: If n is even then n is divisible by 4
If n is not divisible by 4 then n is odd
If n is odd then n is not divisible by 4
n is divisible by 4 iff n is even
quiz.explain: Converse swaps p and q (q→p). It is FALSE (6 is even, not divisible by 4) — converse is not equivalent to the original.

items.explain: False antecedent makes any implication true.

items.prompt: Write the De Morgan equivalent of ¬(admin ∧ onCall).

items.explain: Flip quantifier; negate inner implication via ¬(p→q) ≡ p∧¬q.

items.answer: Yes — q∧¬q is a contradiction (always F), and p∨F ≡ p.

items.prompt: Name the method: assume √3 rational, derive a contradiction.
Prove "if n is odd then n² is odd" directly (one line).
items.explain: Direct: substitute the odd form and factor out 2.
Replace every n by k+1 mechanically.

items.prompt: Which method for "the sum of two rationals is rational"?
Contrapositive of "if x²=4 then x=2 or x=−2"?
items.answer: If x≠2 and x≠−2 then x²≠4.
items.explain: Negate "x=2 or x=−2" with De Morgan: ¬(p∨q) ≡ ¬p∧¬q.

items.prompt: Base case check: is 2^n > n² true at n=5?
items.explain: Always verify the base numerically before the inductive step.

handsOnLab.title: Verify logic by brute force with Python
handsOnLab.brief: You will verify De Morgan’s laws and the contrapositive equivalence by exhaustive truth-table enumeration in Python, then prove a small parity claim both by hand and by exhaustive check. The machine settles every row; your hand proof must agree.
steps: Open python3. Define implies = lambda p,q: (not p) or q.
Enumerate all four (p,q) pairs. For each, compute not (p and q) and (not p) or (not q); assert they are equal on every row — De Morgan verified by brute force.
Repeat for the dual law: not (p or q) vs (not p) and (not q). Assert equality on all rows.
Verify contrapositive: for all rows, implies(p,q) == implies(not q, not p). Print any counterexample (there will be none).
Show the converse is NOT equivalent: find the row where implies(p,q) != implies(q,p). Record it.
Prove by hand on paper: "if n² is odd then n is odd" via contrapositive. Then brute-force check n in range(0,50): assert (n*n % 2 == 1) implies (n % 2 == 1).
Write up: which equivalences held on all rows, the converse counterexample row, and your parity proof.
handsOnLab.deliverable: A short write-up with the brute-force verification output, the converse counterexample, and the hand parity proof.
handsOnLab.checkpoint: All assertions pass; the converse counterexample row is identified; the hand proof matches the brute-force check.

mockTask.q: A policy states: "If the device is unmanaged, then access is denied." Which restatement is logically equivalent?
choices: If access is granted, then the device is managed
If the device is managed, then access is granted
If access is denied, then the device is unmanaged
Devices are either managed or denied
mockTask.explain: Contrapositive (¬q→¬p) is equivalent. The second is the converse, the third the inverse — neither is equivalent.

questions.q: A user's laptop screen flickers only when the lid is moved. Which component is the most likely cause?
choices: Failing inverter cable / display ribbon cable through the hinge
questions.explain: Flicker tied to lid movement points to the display cable flexing at the hinge; drivers and RAM would fail regardless of lid position.

questions.q: A tablet will not connect to the corporate Wi-Fi but connects fine to a phone hotspot. What should you check first?
choices: Whether the tablet supports the corporate network's Wi-Fi security/802.1X requirements
Whether the tablet case is metal
questions.explain: Hotspot success proves the radio works; failure on one specific network points to that network's security or configuration requirements.

questions.q: Which laptop feature lets a technician replace the battery, RAM, and drive without special tools?
choices: Field-replaceable units designed for user/technician service
questions.explain: Serviceable designs expose FRUs; soldered or sealed designs prevent field replacement.

questions.q: A phone overheats and drains quickly after a third-party repair. Which is the most likely cause?
choices: A pinched or damaged battery/thermal assembly from the repair
questions.explain: Sudden thermal/battery behavior right after a repair implicates the repair work itself — typically battery or thermal-pad damage.

questions.q: Which port and protocol does HTTPS use by default?
questions.explain: HTTPS runs over TCP port 443; 80 is HTTP, 53 is DNS, 25 is SMTP.

questions.q: A PC gets a 169.254.x.x address. What does this indicate?
choices: The DHCP server could not be reached, so APIPA assigned a link-local address
questions.explain: 169.254.0.0/16 is APIPA: Windows self-assigns it when no DHCP response arrives.

questions.q: Which cable type is correct for a 40-meter run to a gigabit switch in an office with fluorescent lighting and EMI?
choices: Multimode fiber is the only option
questions.explain: Shielded Cat6A resists EMI and supports 10GbE at distance; fiber works but is overkill for a 40 m office run.

questions.q: A user can ping 8.8.8.8 but cannot browse any website by name. What is the most likely fault?
questions.explain: Pinging an IP proves L3 connectivity; name resolution failing while IPs work isolates the fault to DNS.

questions.q: Which wireless standard operates exclusively in the 6 GHz band?
questions.explain: Wi-Fi 6E (802.11ax extension) added 6 GHz operation; 802.11n is 2.4/5 GHz, ac is 5 GHz.

questions.q: A PC randomly reboots under load but is stable at idle. Temperatures are normal. What should you suspect first?
questions.explain: Reboots under load with normal thermals are the classic signature of a PSU that cannot sustain peak draw.

questions.q: Which RAM type is correct for a modern desktop motherboard with DDR5 slots?
questions.explain: DDR generations are physically keyed differently; a DDR5 board requires DDR5 modules.

questions.q: An NVMe SSD is not detected in BIOS. The slot is M.2. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The M.2 slot is SATA-only and does not support NVMe
The SSD needs a driver installed in BIOS
NVMe drives require a RAID card
questions.explain: Some M.2 slots are keyed/routed for SATA only; an NVMe drive in a SATA-only slot will not appear.

questions.q: Which symptom best indicates a failing hard drive rather than a software issue?
choices: Slow boot times after an update
Repeated clicking sounds and SMART errors
High CPU usage in Task Manager
questions.explain: Clicking (head actuator faults) plus SMART errors are hardware-level failure indicators.

questions.q: A custom build needs to drive 4K video editing. Which component choice matters most?
choices: A discrete GPU with adequate VRAM plus a CPU with enough cores
questions.explain: 4K editing is GPU- and CPU-bound; VRAM and core count determine timeline performance.

questions.q: What is the purpose of a motherboard's CMOS battery?
choices: To power the CPU during sleep
To retain BIOS/UEFI settings and the real-time clock when unplugged
To back up the hard drive
questions.explain: The coin-cell battery preserves firmware settings and RTC time with no mains power.

questions.q: What is the primary difference between Type 1 and Type 2 hypervisors?
choices: Type 1 runs directly on hardware; Type 2 runs on top of a host OS
Type 1 is free; Type 2 is paid
questions.explain: Type 1 (bare-metal, e.g., Hyper-V Server/ESXi) sits on hardware; Type 2 (e.g., VirtualBox) is an application on a host OS.

questions.q: A company wants to move CapEx to OpEx and scale resources on demand. Which cloud model fits?
questions.explain: Public cloud converts capital expense to operational expense with elastic scaling.

questions.q: Which is a key resource requirement to verify before deploying VMs on a host?
choices: Available CPU, RAM, storage IOPS, and network bandwidth versus VM demand
questions.explain: VM density planning requires matching aggregate VM demand against host compute, memory, storage, and network capacity.

questions.q: What is the correct FIRST step in the standard troubleshooting methodology?
choices: Identify the problem: gather information and question users
questions.explain: Methodology starts with identifying the problem before theorizing or acting.

questions.q: After implementing a fix, what is the required next step?
choices: Verify full system functionality and implement preventive measures
questions.explain: Verification plus preventive measures (and documentation) complete the methodology.

questions.q: A printer prints blank pages. Ink/toner is full. What is the most likely cause?
choices: Protective tape/seal left on the cartridge or a clogged printhead
questions.explain: Full consumables plus blank output points to the transfer path: unremoved seals or clogged heads.

questions.q: Intermittent network drops affect one workstation. Swapping the patch cable fixes it permanently. What was the fault?
choices: A damaged or marginal patch cable
questions.explain: Single-host intermittent issues resolved by cable swap implicate the cable itself.

questions.q: A PC shows no display but fans spin and drives sound active. What should you check first?
choices: Monitor cable, input source, and reseat RAM/GPU
questions.explain: No-display-with-power is most often cable/input or a POST-stopping reseat issue; check the simple external causes first.

questions.q: Which tool verifies that a cable run is wired to the correct pinout standard?
questions.explain: A cable tester checks continuity and correct pin-to-pin mapping.

questions.q: A laptop battery swells and the trackpad lifts. What is the correct action?
choices: Puncture the battery to release pressure
Power down, do not charge or puncture, and replace the battery following safety procedures
Keep using it until it dies
questions.explain: Swollen lithium batteries are a fire hazard: stop use, never puncture, replace per safety procedure.

questions.q: Which Windows tool shows startup programs, services, and boot configuration?
questions.explain: msconfig manages boot options, services, and startup items.

questions.q: A user needs to join a Windows Pro machine to a domain. Where is this done?
choices: System Properties > Computer Name > Change > Domain
questions.explain: Domain membership is set in System Properties under Computer Name/Domain Changes.

questions.q: Which command-line tool displays the IP configuration of a Windows host?
questions.explain: ipconfig shows addresses, mask, gateway, and DNS for each adapter.

questions.q: What does the `chkdsk /r` command do?
choices: Locates bad sectors and recovers readable information while checking disk integrity
questions.explain: /r implies /f plus a full surface scan for bad sectors with data recovery.

questions.q: Which Windows feature allows rolling back a faulty driver update?
questions.explain: Device Manager's Roll Back Driver reverts to the previously installed driver.

questions.q: A workstation cannot reach a file share by name but can by IP. Which OS-level setting should you verify?
choices: The DNS server addresses on the adapter
questions.explain: Name resolution for shares depends on DNS (or NetBIOS); IP access working isolates it to name resolution.

questions.q: Which partition style is required to boot Windows from a disk larger than 2 TB?
questions.explain: GPT supports disks over 2 TB and UEFI boot; MBR is limited to 2 TB.

questions.q: What is the purpose of Windows Safe Mode?
choices: Booting with minimal drivers/services to diagnose problems
questions.explain: Safe Mode loads a minimal driver set so faulty drivers or software can be isolated.

questions.q: Which is the strongest password policy control against brute-force attacks?
choices: Account lockout after failed attempts plus complexity and length requirements
questions.explain: Lockout throttles guessing; complexity and length raise the search space.

questions.q: A user receives an email asking for credentials with a link to a lookalike domain. This is:
questions.explain: Credential harvesting via deceptive email and lookalike domains is phishing.

questions.q: Which Windows feature encrypts an entire drive to protect data if a laptop is stolen?
questions.explain: BitLocker provides full-disk encryption tied to TPM/PIN.

questions.q: What is the principle of least privilege?
choices: Grant users only the access required to do their jobs
questions.explain: Least privilege minimizes the blast radius of compromised accounts.

questions.q: Which is the best practice when disposing of a hard drive containing sensitive data?
choices: Degauss/destroy or cryptographically wipe per policy
questions.explain: Sensitive media requires verifiable destruction or wiping, never casual disposal.

questions.q: What does MFA protect against that a strong password alone does not?
choices: Credential theft/replay, since the attacker also needs the second factor
questions.explain: A second factor means a stolen password alone is insufficient.

questions.q: What is the correct order for malware remediation?
choices: Investigate, quarantine, disable System Restore, remediate, schedule scans, enable Restore, educate user
questions.explain: The standard sequence isolates the threat, removes it safely, and prevents reinfection.

questions.q: An application crashes on launch after an update. What is the best FIRST step?
choices: Check the application and OS event logs for the error
questions.explain: Logs identify the faulting module before any destructive action.

questions.q: A PC is extremely slow. Task Manager shows 100% disk usage from one process. What next?
choices: Identify the process; check for runaway indexing, AV scan, or failing drive, then act
questions.explain: Diagnose the specific consumer first — cause determines the fix.

questions.q: Which symptom most suggests a corrupted OS rather than a bad application?
choices: Multiple unrelated system functions fail and SFC finds integrity violations
questions.explain: System-wide failures plus SFC integrity violations point at OS corruption.

questions.q: What does Windows System Restore do?
choices: Reverts system files, drivers, and registry to a restore point without touching personal files
questions.explain: System Restore rolls back system state; personal files are preserved.

questions.q: A mobile app drains battery rapidly in the background. What is the best first step?
choices: Check battery usage stats, restrict background activity for the offending app
questions.explain: Battery stats identify the consumer; restricting its background activity is the targeted fix.

questions.q: Before opening a plugged-in desktop case, what must you do first?
choices: Power off, unplug, and use ESD protection
questions.explain: Unplug plus ESD strap prevents shock and electrostatic damage.

questions.q: A toner spill occurs. What is the correct cleanup?
choices: Use a toner-rated (HEPA/ESD-safe) vacuum; never a standard vacuum
Blow it with compressed air toward your face
questions.explain: Standard vacuums can ignite fine toner or blow it through; toner vacuums are filtered and ESD-safe.

questions.q: Which document records what changed, when, and why for IT systems?
questions.explain: Change records provide auditability and rollback reference.

questions.q: A user is upset about downtime. What is the professional response?
choices: Argue about whose fault it is
Acknowledge the impact, communicate status and ETA, and follow up
questions.explain: Professionalism: empathy, clear status, committed follow-up.

questions.q: Why should you document lessons learned after resolving a major incident?
choices: So the next technician can resolve it faster and preventive measures can be implemented
questions.explain: Documentation converts one incident into institutional knowledge and prevention.
